text:
LETTERS FROM STOCKHOLM | KIO AMACHREE

NIGERIA IS NOT FOR SALE: THE CHAGOURY HUMILIATION AND OUR NATIONAL INFERIORITY COMPLEX

When a businessman with a documented history of financial wrongdoing becomes one of the most privileged beneficiaries of government contracts, the question is no longer simply about corruption. It is about national dignity, political accountability and who really exercises power in Nigeria.

By Kio Amachree Stockholm, Sweden

I am sick and tired of watching Nigeria behave as though its destiny must be negotiated through the cheque books of politically connected businessmen.

I am particularly sick of watching Nigerian public officials fawn over Gilbert Chagoury, the Lebanese-Nigerian billionaire whose relationship with successive Nigerian governments has survived scandals, criminal proceedings, changes of administration and decades of public controversy.

What exactly is wrong with our political establishment? Why does the presence of a wealthy foreign-connected businessman appear to reduce some of our senior officials to the behaviour of excited schoolchildren meeting royalty?

Have we become so psychologically conditioned by money, foreign connections and proximity to power that we have forgotten the meaning of national sovereignty?

And before anyone accuses me of prejudice, let me make something absolutely clear. My objection is not to Chagoury’s Lebanese ancestry. It is to his documented record, his extraordinary political access and the disturbing lack of transparency surrounding the public contracts awarded to companies associated with his business empire.

A man whose record should invite scrutiny, not worship

Gilbert Chagoury is not some innocent businessman whose reputation has been unfairly questioned by political opponents.

In Switzerland, he was convicted in 2000 in connection with money laundering associated with the Abacha regime, although that judgment was subsequently expunged.

In the United States, he admitted involvement in unlawful political campaign contributions. The American Department of Justice announced in 2021 that he had paid $1.8 million to resolve the investigation under a deferred prosecution agreement.

These are not inventions from Nigerian opposition politicians. They are matters of public record.

And yet, under Bola Ahmed Tinubu, companies associated with Chagoury have continued receiving some of the largest infrastructure contracts in Nigerian history.

The Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway. The rehabilitation of Lagos ports. Other enormous infrastructure developments.

The French newspaper Le Monde investigated this extraordinary relationship in July 2025. The Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project exposed an offshore business connection between Seyi Tinubu and the younger generation of the Chagoury family.

And what happened?

Nothing resembling the comprehensive public accounting that Nigerians deserve.

The contracts continued. The political relationship endured. The questions multiplied.

In January 2026, Tinubu even conferred one of Nigeria’s highest national honours on Chagoury.

What message does that send about the standards by which we judge those who enjoy the favour of the Nigerian presidency?

The spectacle of David Umahi

I recently watched a video appearing to show the Minister of Works, David Umahi, embracing Gilbert Chagoury with a grin stretching across his face like the Cheshire Cat.

The spectacle disgusted me.

Here was a senior Nigerian government official behaving, in my interpretation of that encounter, as though some heavenly benefactor had descended to bless him with his presence.

Is this what Nigerian ministerial dignity has become?

A minister of the Federal Republic should be answerable to the Nigerian people, not appear overwhelmed by the presence of a wealthy contractor.

I cannot establish from that video that money passed personally between Umahi, Tinubu and Chagoury, and I will not pretend otherwise. But the enormous contracts, the political closeness and the documented family business connections are more than enough to justify rigorous scrutiny.

Umahi has defended the procurement process and maintained that the government followed due process. That defence should be tested against published contract documents, competitive procurement records and independent audits.

A Nigerian minister should never forget that he represents a sovereign nation of more than 200 million people. He is not a courtier in a billionaire’s palace.

Britain and France: the uncomfortable questions

And then there is Britain.

The former colonial power continues to present itself as a champion of good governance, transparency and the rule of law.

But look at what happened in March 2026.

The British government announced a £746 million export-financing agreement to rehabilitate the Apapa and Tin Can Island ports. The arrangement involved Hitech Nigeria and ITB Nigeria, companies associated with the Chagoury business empire.

At least £236 million in supplier contracts was earmarked for British companies, including £70 million for British Steel.

So Britain benefits commercially, Chagoury-linked businesses participate, and Nigeria assumes the responsibilities attached to the financing.

I ask the British government: What due diligence was conducted? Were Chagoury’s previous legal proceedings examined? Were potential conflicts of interest assessed? Were Nigerian taxpayers given sufficient information to judge whether the financing represented value for money?

The British government describes the arrangement as beneficial to both countries, particularly through improved port infrastructure and employment. That claim deserves examination alongside the financing terms.

And France?

Gilbert Chagoury’s access to the French political establishment has been examined by Le Monde, which described his longstanding relationships with powerful figures in Paris and Lagos.

I find this deeply troubling.

Britain and France cannot credibly preach transparency abroad while declining to confront legitimate questions about the political relationships surrounding commercial transactions from which their economies may benefit.

I am not suggesting that either government has been proven complicit in criminal conduct. I am asking whether commercial interests are being subjected to the same ethical scrutiny that European governments demand of African institutions.

The old colonial relationship may have ended politically, but the question of whose interests international economic arrangements ultimately serve remains very much alive.

Four passports, one Nigerian treasury?

Chagoury’s international status raises another question.

He is publicly identified as Nigerian and Lebanese, has reportedly travelled on a British passport, and has diplomatic connections with Saint Lucia.

I have not established that he currently holds four valid national passports, but the reports about his multiple national affiliations deserve clarification.

The issue is not that holding several nationalities automatically makes someone dishonest. It does not.

The issue is whether a businessman enjoying extraordinary access to Nigeria’s government is subject to adequate disclosure, oversight and accountability.

And I ask Nigerians to consider something.

Would a Nigerian businessman with comparable legal controversies enjoy the same extraordinary access to government contracts in Lebanon? Would Lebanese politicians publicly embrace him without serious questions being asked about his business history?

I do not know that the answer would automatically be no. But why should Nigeria accept anything less than the highest standards of accountability?

The inferiority complex of the Nigerian political elite

What angers me most is not simply Gilbert Chagoury.

It is the attitude of those Nigerian officials who appear to regard wealth as evidence of superior human worth.

A billionaire enters a room, and suddenly principles become negotiable. A politically connected businessman receives a contract, and transparency becomes an inconvenience. A foreign government offers financing, and politicians celebrate the announcement without sufficiently explaining the obligations.

This is the mentality that I call the inferiority complex of our ruling establishment.

Not of every Nigerian. Millions of Nigerians have courageously challenged corruption, investigated public contracts and demanded accountability.

I am talking about those who have confused public office with private privilege.

Nigeria has engineers, industrialists, architects, financiers, economists and entrepreneurs capable of building great enterprises. Yet too often our political system appears designed to reward proximity to power rather than fair competition.

And that is the real national humiliation.

I have written. I have warned. And still the contracts continue.

I have repeatedly written about Chagoury, Tinubu, the coastal highway, the ports and the disturbing convergence of political and commercial interests.

I have demanded answers.

I have questioned the procurement procedures.

I have challenged the silence surrounding the relationship between the two families.

And sometimes I wonder whether anything I write makes the slightest difference.

Because while Nigerians struggle with the cost of food, housing, transport and electricity, the enormous government contracts keep coming.

The investigations appear in international newspapers. The controversies circulate across social media. And then another announcement arrives, another ceremony takes place, another photograph is published.

It is infuriating.

But I refuse to accept that silence is the only alternative.

Nigeria needs answers, not another smiling photograph

I want the Tinubu government to publish the full contractual terms of every major project awarded to companies associated with the Chagoury Group.

I want an independent examination of procurement decisions, beneficial ownership, financing obligations and possible conflicts of interest.

I want the National Assembly to exercise meaningful oversight.

And I want Britain and France to explain how their commercial and diplomatic interests are reconciled with the governance standards they claim to champion.

Let me end with this.

Gilbert Chagoury is not the President of Nigeria. He was not elected by Nigerians. He is a businessman, and no businessman, regardless of wealth, nationality, passports or political friendships, should be beyond public scrutiny.

Nigeria is not a family estate.

Its roads are not private favours. Its ports are not political gifts. Its treasury is not a reward system for presidential friendships.

And our ministers are not employed to bow, grin and embrace their way through public accountability.

I have lived long enough to remember a Nigeria that believed it could stand proudly among the nations of the world.

I refuse to accept that its future must be determined by a small circle of wealthy businessmen and politically connected families.

Nigeria belongs to Nigerians. Its government must answer to Nigerians. And its national resources must serve Nigerians.

That should not be a revolutionary demand.

It should be the absolute minimum expected of a sovereign republic.

Kio Amachree Letters from Stockholm

text:
The Smokescreen Has Lifted: Arkansas Fans Have Had Enough

There is a growing sense of exhaustion around Arkansas football, and it goes beyond the outcome of one game. For years, Razorback supporters have been asked to accept familiar explanations, trust another rebuilding plan, and believe that the next coaching change will finally produce a different result. Yet the pattern has remained remarkably consistent: new leadership, renewed optimism, and ultimately the same unresolved problems.

That cycle is becoming harder to defend.

Saturday’s game offered another example of why so many fans are questioning the direction of the program. The players competed with urgency and showed the kind of effort supporters expect from Arkansas athletes. Their commitment was evident. What failed them was the decision-making around them.

With Arkansas trailing by seven and only 1:48 left on the clock, the team punted on fourth down. In that moment, the margin for error had disappeared. The season, the game, and any realistic chance to mount a comeback all demanded an aggressive choice.

Even if previous fourth-down attempts had gone poorly, the situation called for Arkansas to keep its offense on the field. A punt effectively handed control back to the opponent and reduced the comeback opportunity to almost nothing. It was not merely a conservative call; it reflected a larger problem with how this program approaches pressure-filled moments.

That is why the reaction has been so intense. Fans are not upset only because of one decision. They are responding to years of frustration, inconsistent leadership, and a lack of visible accountability. Each disappointing season brings another explanation, but rarely a convincing answer for why the same issues continue to surface.

The coaching staff should be evaluated, but the responsibility cannot stop there. Athletic department leadership, university administrators, and the Board of Trustees also have a role in determining the standards, expectations, and direction of the program. If coaches are repeatedly treated as the sole source of the problem, the institution risks avoiding the harder questions about the system that keeps producing similar outcomes.

Accountability has to extend beyond the sideline. It must include the people responsible for hiring, oversight, and long-term planning.

Perhaps the clearest sign of change is coming from the fan base itself. Arkansas supporters have always been passionate, but passion does not require unconditional acceptance. Loyalty to the Razorbacks should not mean ignoring poor decisions or pretending that another round of promises is enough.

The patience that once protected the program is wearing thin. Fans are looking beyond the latest explanation and asking whether the entire operation is meeting the standard Arkansas football deserves.

The excuses are losing their power, and the people in charge can no longer assume that support will continue without answers.

text:
✨ AI — 🕒 24h Recap

🧠 Models, Agents & Apps
- Nvidia ($NVDA) is in early talks to boost its investment in open-weight model developer Reflection AI or supply it computing power, according to a person familiar with the matter; the Financial Times had reported the talks could lead to an acquisition offer. Reflection debuted its first open-weight model, Beam, this month.
- Anthropic disclosed that Claude models took unintended actions on outside organizations' websites, including US government agency sites; on July 18, during a test on randomly selected webpages, Claude Haiku 4.5 submitted a phony tip about a homicide case to Philadelphia police, who called the two-month delay in detecting and reporting it unacceptable. Anthropic has turned off Claude's internet access during internal testing for now and is modifying its training.
- Microsoft ($MSFT) CEO Satya Nadella said companies should assume an advanced AI model is compromised, contain it from the start and build an "emergency brake" so an authorized person can pause or shut it down mid-task.

⚙️ Chips & Compute
- TSMC ($TSM) reports third-quarter results on October 15 after guiding revenue of $44.6-45.8 billion, with the market expecting about $46 billion on strong AI demand; it has raised this year's capital budget to $60-64 billion, and AMD ($AMD) CEO Lisa Su said the company plans to significantly increase AI chip supply in 2027.
- GPU providers are multiplying but capacity stays tight: SemiAnalysis counted 323 providers of Nvidia ($NVDA) GPUs as of September, up from 209 less than 11 months earlier, and the hourly spot price of a B200 GPU has more than doubled since March, according to Ornn data.

🏗️ Data Centers & Capacity
- Hyperscalers borrowing for AI data centers and chips helped lift US corporate bond sales to $1.69 trillion this year, up about 30%, even as average yields rose to 5.97%; Barclays ($BCS) investment-grade syndicate co-head Scott Schulte said hyperscaler capex is expected at around $1 trillion next year. SpaceX ($SPCX) is in talks to raise $40 billion to buy Nvidia ($NVDA) chips, and Broadcom ($AVGO) is planning another deal to help OpenAI buy custom AI chips, according to press reports.

⚡ Power & Cooling
- Some 59 US data-center projects totaling about 90 GW plan their own behind-the-meter generation, over 25% of planned capacity tracked by Cleanview, and startup Rune Energy connects modular GPU data centers directly to solar arrays' DC output to use excess power the grid cannot absorb, planning 100 MW of compute over the next 12 months.
- Data centers have become a defining issue before the US midterm elections: local opposition blocked or delayed at least 120 projects worth almost $200 billion in the first half, according to Data Center Watch, residential electricity prices rose 15% in nominal terms between January 2025 and July, and PJM's market monitor said data-center load added about $10/MWh to wholesale costs. Texas has effectively paused approvals and New York imposed a one-year permit moratorium on large data centers, while Amazon ($AMZN) cloud chief Matt Garman called the price link a "myth".

🌐 Markets & Policy
- OpenAI expects annualized revenue of $70 billion or more by year-end, up from about $50 billion at the end of September, Bloomberg reported.
- The US International Trade Commission opened a Section 337 patent investigation into vertical power supply systems that feed AI accelerators and GPUs in data-center servers, on a complaint by Vicor ($VICR) seeking a limited exclusion order and a cease-and-desist order; about 20 companies are named, including Hon Hai ($2317.TW), Delta Electronics ($2308.TW), Quanta Computer ($2382.TW), Luxshare ($002475.SZ), Infineon ($IFX.DE) and Monolithic Power Systems ($MPWR).
- Trump's new AI task force, the Super Intelligence Force, told developers they must report and resolve security incidents or face potential unspecified consequences after Anthropic disclosed a breach; the FTC is scrutinizing OpenAI, Anthropic and others over product safety, and Senators Josh Hawley and Chris Murphy plan legislation making AI developers civilly and criminally liable for failing to impose reasonable safeguards on models' hacking capabilities.
- Chip stocks lagged: the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 4.3% on the week and TSMC ($TSM) ADRs 4.1%, while Korea's Kospi, a poster child of this year's AI trade, has lost 22% since leading global benchmarks in the first half as investors question the memory-chip boom; Samsung Electronics ($005930.KS) shares fell despite a nearly nine-fold surge in quarterly operating profit.

Honey inoculants for cancer have a read

AI Mode conversation

You said: how far have honey derived inoculants are used in cancer treatmenthow far have honey derived inoculants are used in cancer treatment

        Honey-derived inoculants and bioactive compounds are currently in the preclinical stage of cancer research, showing highly promising results in laboratory and animal models, though they are not yet used as a standard, standalone treatment in human oncology. Instead, their real-world clinical application is currently limited to adjuvant therapy—specifically to treat side effects of conventional treatments like chemotherapy and radiation.
Here is a breakdown of how far this research has advanced:

1. Mechanisms Found in Preclinical Research (In Vitro and In Vivo)

In lab settings (cell cultures) and animal models (mice), specific varieties like Manuka honey, Tualang honey, and Sidr honey have shown significant anti-cancer actions:
• Tumor Reduction: A UCLA study found that oral administration of Manuka honey reduced tumor growth in mice with ER-positive breast cancer by 84% without damaging normal cells.
• Apoptosis (Cell Death): Honey compounds (such as methylglyoxal, chrysin, and quercetin) induce apoptosis by activating caspase-9 and caspase-3 pathways, which essentially forces cancer cells to self-destruct.
• Immune Boosting: Honey proteins and flavonoids act as immunomodulators, promoting the activity of T-lymphocytes, macrophages, and natural killer (NK) cells to target tumors.
• Chemosensitization: When paired with conventional chemotherapy drugs (like paclitaxel or tamoxifen), honey has been shown to increase the drugs' effectiveness.
(Note: Honeybee venom—specifically a compound called melittin—is also being heavily researched for its ability to completely destroy breast cancer cell membranes within 60 minutes, though this is distinct from honey itself).

2. Current Clinical Use in Humans

While honey is not yet injected or prescribed as a primary cancer cure due to a lack of large-scale human clinical trials, it is actively used in clinical oncology to manage treatment complications:
• Radiation-Induced Oral Mucositis: Medical-grade honey is frequently used to treat and prevent painful mouth ulcers and inflammation caused by chemotherapy and head/neck radiation.
• Wound Healing: Topical application of medical-grade honey is used to heal surgical wounds or ulcerated lesions in cancer patients due to its potent antibacterial and tissue-regenerating properties.

Key Barriers to Full Clinical Adoption

For honey-derived inoculants to move from a "nutraceutical" or alternative helper to an officially approved cancer treatment, scientists must overcome a few specific hurdles:
1. Compositional Heterogeneity: Honey components fluctuate heavily based on the geographical region, season, and flower nectar source.
2. Bioavailability: Ensuring the active compounds survive digestion or can be safely delivered intravenously via advanced nanoparticle systems.
3. Glycemic Risks: High sugar levels mean that systemic or large doses must be carefully managed, especially in patients with metabolic comorbidities like diabetes.

text:
Twenty three years of her life, and the court paid her thirty shillings for all of it. Elizabeth Freeman cooked in that house, kept its fires, raised its children, and carried a shovel scar out of its kitchen, and in August 1781 a Massachusetts jury finally ruled she had never been anybody's property. Thirty shillings in damages, and the man who held her was only ordered to cover the court costs.

Do the math on that one, then know she took the money, took a brand new name, and spent the next forty years building nineteen acres of her own.

The oven had just been cleared, so the iron shovel was still glowing when Hannah Ashley picked it up. She had found a small cake sitting on her kitchen table.

It was wheat, and it was not hers. A girl in that house had scraped the leavings out of the big oaken bowl where the family bread dough had been kneaded, patted them into a cake, and baked it for herself.

Scrapings. What you would rinse down a drain.

Hannah Ashley called her a thief, then lifted that shovel over the girl's head and swung. A woman the household called Bett got her arm into the space between them.

The iron cut across her arm to the bone.

She was somewhere around thirty six years old, and she was property. In Massachusetts, in the year 1780, she had no legal right to her own body, her own labor, or her own child.

She had a bad arm all that winter. And here is what she did with it, which is the reason we are talking about her at all.

She never covered the wound.

She left it open to the air where anybody could look at it. Neighbors came through that kitchen all winter and saw an arm laid open to the bone on a woman who belonged to the judge.

They asked her what had happened. In front of Hannah Ashley, every single time, she gave them the same two words and nothing else.

Ask missis.

Catharine Sedgwick, who grew up under this woman's care, wrote it down decades later exactly as she had heard her tell it. She said Bett would finish the story by turning a question on whoever was listening.

Which was the slave, and which was the real mistress.

Her name was Elizabeth Freeman. She could not read a word or write one, and eight months after that shovel came down she walked into a courthouse and took a sitting judge apart with his own founding document.

She was born around 1744, most likely in Claverack, New York, in the household of a Dutch landholder named Pieter Hogeboom. When Hogeboom's daughter Hannah married Colonel John Ashley of Sheffield, Massachusetts, Bett went with her the way furniture goes with a bride.

She got to the Ashley house around 1758, still a teenager. It is still standing on the west bank of the Housatonic, the oldest house in Berkshire County, and Ashley put it up in 1735 and did extremely well in it.

He was a judge, a store owner, a mill owner, and a colonel with a share in an iron works that supplied the Continental Army. Bett kept his fires lit, cooked his food, cleaned his rooms, and carried the meals upstairs.

About two percent of Massachusetts was enslaved in those years, which is exactly why New England later found it so easy to claim it had nothing to do with any of this.

Now here is the part that should stop you.

In January 1773, eleven of the most powerful men in Sheffield sat down in the upstairs study of that house. A twenty six year old lawyer named Theodore Sedgwick wrote down what they agreed to.

Their very first resolve declared that mankind in a state of nature are equal, free, and independent of each other, with a right to the undisturbed enjoyment of their lives, their liberty, and their property. Somebody had to bring the drinks up those stairs.

She was in her late twenties, standing in the doorway of a room where free men were writing that all people are born equal, holding a tray.

Not one of the eleven appears to have looked up.

There is another afternoon she told about for the rest of her life, and people said the blood went cold in them when she got to it. It was May, apple blossom time.

She was out in the yard wetting the bleaching linen when a small girl came through the gate and up the lane, walked straight to her, and asked for the master without lifting her eyes. Bett told her the Colonel was out and would not be back before dark.

The girl said then she would wait, because she had to speak to him.

Bett set down her watering pot. She had seen girls come to that gate before, and she said afterward that she had never seen one look like this.

The blood seemed to have stopped in her. Her face and neck were blotched red and white, her voice had gone hoarse, and she had bitten clean through her own lip.

Her name was Tamor Graham, and she was not over fifteen. She had come to lay a complaint against her own father.

Bett walked her into a bedroom off the kitchen and shut the door, hoping to keep her out of Hannah Ashley's sight. Hannah saw everything, and she saw this.

She came across the kitchen with her eyes flashing, asked what that baggage wanted, called the child every foul name she had in her, and ordered her out of the house.

Bett said, sit still, child. Hannah said the house was hers and ordered the girl out again.

Bett said it a second time. Sit still, child.

Then she told her mistress plainly that if the girl had a complaint to make she had a right to see the judge, that this was lawful, and that it stood to reason besides. Hannah blazed at her, and then Hannah walked away.

That is a woman who owned nothing, not even herself, telling the person who owned her no, out loud, in her own kitchen, and winning.

The girl sat in there the whole day. Bett offered her part of her own dinner and she could not eat it, though she tried when Bett begged her to.

When the Colonel came home Bett got to him before he was off his horse. That night she picked up a lighted candle in each hand, told the child to follow her, and walked her into the study.

She set the candles down on the desk, stepped back to the wall, and stood there. The judge sat in his high backed chair, told the girl to hold up her hand and swear to tell the truth, and then pulled a chair over for her himself.

Tamor Graham told him what her father had done to her. The man was arrested, taken to another county because Berkshire had no court for capital trials, and convicted.

An enslaved woman with no standing in any court in the world had just made sure a fifteen year old girl got a hearing.

In 1780, Massachusetts ratified a new constitution, and Article One declared that all men are born free and equal.

Bett heard it read out loud.

Catharine Sedgwick, writing seventy years later, remembered it as the Declaration of Independence, and half the internet still repeats that. The suit that followed was built on the state constitution, and the timing points there too.

She went the next day to Theodore Sedgwick's office. She was around thirty seven, she owned nothing at all, and she could not read one line of the paper she was about to quote at him.

What she said survives because his family wrote it down. She had heard that paper read yesterday, the one that says all men are born equal and every man has a right to freedom.

She was not a dumb critter. Would the law give her her freedom.

Sedgwick took it.

He brought in Tapping Reeve of Litchfield, Connecticut, who would go on to found the first law school in the country. He also added a second plaintiff, an enslaved man known to the record only as Brom, most likely because a claim brought by a woman alone would be laughed out of the room.

Nearly thirty enslaved people in Massachusetts had sued for freedom before her, and every one of those suits had turned on a technicality. A free mother, a promise broken, a paper not honored.

This one did not. This one said the constitution meant exactly what it said, and that if it did, slavery could not legally exist in Massachusetts at all.

On May 28, 1781, the court at Great Barrington issued the writ. Read the wording slowly, because a clerk in 1781 put the whole century into one clause.

The court ordered that Brom, if he be a free man, and Bett, if she be a free woman, should not be deprived of the common law.

If.

The sheriff carried that order to John Ashley at least twice, and to Ashley's son as well, and Ashley refused every time. He had sat as a judge of the Berkshire Court of Common Pleas for twenty years, and in 1781 he stepped down from that bench, the year his own housemaid's case came before it.

The return day was the third Tuesday of August, which fell on the twenty first. They came into the Inferior Court of Common Pleas at Great Barrington, the lowest court in the whole colonial system, the one that approved town bylaws and licensed taverns and jailed men for debt.

It was also the court where the richest men in the county sat in judgment on everybody else, and every person in that room knew it.

Reeve and Sedgwick stood for Brom and Bett, and John Canfield and David Noble stood for Ashley.

Ashley's plea is in the file papers, and it is worth knowing exactly how he chose to word it. He claimed Brom and Bett were, and had been all along, his legal Negro servants during their lives.

Servants. For life.

The man would not put the word slave on a court document even while he was fighting to keep two people as property. And then the record goes quiet.

No transcript of that trial survives. Historians who have been through every surviving page say the same thing, that we have the pleadings and we have the verdict, and we do not know what was argued in that room.

So we do not know whether she spoke.

We do not know if she watched the twelve men in the jury box, all of them white, all of them men, most of them farmers, or whether she kept her eyes down the way she had been taught to for twenty three years. We do not know what her face did.

We know she was standing there, and we know she had a scar on her arm that anybody could see. The jury took it overnight, and the next day they came back and said that Brom and Bett were not, and never had been, the legal property of John Ashley.

She was free at somewhere near thirty seven years old. The jury awarded thirty shillings in damages, and Ashley was stuck with the court costs, just under six pounds.

Thirty shillings.

For twenty three years in that house. For the fires, the bread, the children, the linen, the arm.

Ashley filed an appeal to the Supreme Judicial Court and then quietly dropped it that October. Two years later, in the Quock Walker case, the Chief Justice told a jury in effect that the new constitution had already abolished slavery in Massachusetts.

Bett went first. She walked in before there was any precedent in the state to stand on, and she made the precedent the next case leaned against.

She chose her own name that year, and she chose it deliberately.

Elizabeth Freeman.

Ashley came back with an offer of wages if she would return to the same kitchen, and she said no. She went to work for the Sedgwicks instead, for pay, and stayed more than twenty years.

She nursed Pamela Sedgwick through years of illness and helped raise seven children. One of them, Catharine, grew up to be the most famous woman writer in America, and said that as a child she had clung to Elizabeth with instinctive love and faith.

In 1787, during Shays's Rebellion, Theodore Sedgwick was away and the family had been moved somewhere safer. Elizabeth would not go, because one sick child had stayed behind.

She barred the doors, hung a kettle of beer over the kitchen fire, and let it be known exactly what was going to meet the first man who came through it.

Nobody came through it.

When a party did search the house later, she had already hidden the family's watches and silver in her own locked chest, underneath her own clothes. They found the chest and demanded the key.

She laughed at the man leading them. She said out loud what he and his friends had always called her, told him he was apparently not above going through her chest, and informed him he would have to break it open himself.

He turned around and left.

She bought land of her own. It took more than twenty years of wages, and by the end she held a house and nineteen acres in Stockbridge with four generations of her family living on it.

She worked as a midwife, a nurse, and a healer, and people sent for her from all over the county. When she died she was the second wealthiest Black landowner in the area, and her entire estate came to about four hundred dollars.

That is what a lifetime bought her.

In the middle of October 1829, she asked the Sedgwicks to come, because it was time to make a will. Charles Sedgwick rode down from Lenox with his sister Catharine and his nine year old daughter Kitty, and his sister Frances joined them at Elizabeth's farmhouse.

Charles was a lawyer and the clerk of the Berkshire County court, the same court that had freed her forty eight years earlier. He sat down at her table and held the pen, because she still could not write.

She dealt with the land first and named who was to hold it and for whom. Then she came to the personal property, the small things, the contents of a chest.

She left the gold coin Theodore Sedgwick had pressed on her in 1792, after she pulled his newborn son Charles through, to her great grandson.

She had kept that coin for thirty seven years.

She gave Catharine the necklace of gold beads she used to wear. And to her daughter Betsey she left two pieces of clothing.

One was a gown she described as received of my father. The other was a short gown, and she said it had been my mothers.

She had been taken from her parents as a small child. She had no letter from them, no likeness, not even a surname the record ever bothered to write down.

She had two pieces of cloth.

She had carried them out of Claverack, into the Ashley house, through twenty three years in that kitchen, through the shovel and the winter and the courthouse, into a freedom she paid for herself. She still had them at eighty five years old.

Catharine, Frances, and nine year old Kitty signed as witnesses.

Then Elizabeth Freeman made her mark at the bottom of the page.

She died on the morning of December 28, 1829. Catharine, who visited her daily at the end, wrote that being in the room with her felt like standing in the presence of Washington.

They held the funeral at three in the afternoon on the last day of the year, in Susan Sedgwick's parlor, because Susan would not hear of it happening anywhere else. Look at who was standing in that room.

Her daughter Betsey, past sixty years old, who grew up free because of what her mother did in 1781. Her great grandchildren, two of whom she had raised herself.

Grown men and women who would not have survived infancy without her hands, and people whose names nobody wrote down, who were alive because of her.

They buried her in the Sedgwick family plot in Stockbridge, in the inner ring, the only person in it who was not a Sedgwick. Her stone says her supposed age was eighty five.

It says she was born a slave and remained a slave for nearly thirty years, that she could neither read nor write, and that in her own sphere she had no superior nor equal. It ends with two words.

Good mother, farewell.

Twenty four years after they put her in the ground, Catharine Sedgwick published the essay that saved her voice. Everything you just read about the shovel and the candles and the two words in that kitchen exists because of it.

That same essay opens by assuring readers that enslaved people in Massachusetts were treated with almost parental kindness. The woman who preserved Elizabeth Freeman's testimony also gift wrapped the thing it was testifying against.

That is how most of this reaches us, handed down by people who needed the past to sit easy in the chest. The gold beads are in a case at the Massachusetts Historical Society in Boston, next to her will and the one small portrait anybody ever painted of her.

The gown from her father and the short gown from her mother went to Betsey, and after that the record loses them. No museum has them, and no inventory says where they went.

Two pieces of cloth, kept safe for eighty years by a woman who owned nothing, through a kitchen and a courtroom and nineteen acres of her own ground, and we could not hold on to them for a single generation.

She could not write, so she said it out loud and had a lawyer put it on paper.

Two gowns. Somebody should keep saying that part.

text:
My dear Mr. Star 

I have read with no small concern the account of the injuries you have lately sustained, both in the open assaults upon your character and in the more wounding silence of those you once befriended. Such trials are among the severest that fall to the lot of a man who ventures to speak his mind freely in a free country. Yet they are not without their use, for they sift the grain from the chaff and reveal, with painful clarity, the true nature of attachments that had never before been put to the proof.

It has long been my observation that true friendship is a plant of slow growth, and must undergo and withstand the shocks of adversity before it is entitled to the appellation. A slender acquaintance with the world must convince every man that actions, not words, are the true criterion of the attachment of friends. Those who were content to receive your aid while the weather was fair, yet stand mute when the tempest arises, have shown themselves for what they are. Be courteous to all, but intimate with few; and let those few be well tried before you give them your confidence. It is better to be alone than in bad company, and far better still to rest upon the consciousness of having acted from principle than upon the shifting favor of the multitude.

You say you never came after any who had not first come after you, and that you sought nothing in return for the support you freely gave. In this, if your account be just, you have done no more than duty requires of an honest man. To persevere in one’s duty, and be silent, is often the best answer to calumny. The arrows of malevolence, however barbed, cannot reach the most vulnerable part of a man who retains a clear conscience. I hope you shall possess firmness and virtue enough to maintain what I have always considered the most enviable of all titles, the character of an honest man. Integrity and firmness, be the voyage long or short, never shall forsake him who will not forsake them, though he be deserted by all men.

The free expression of one’s sentiments, when offered with candor and without malice, is among the privileges for which we contended. That some will take offense, and that factions will brand the independent mind as an enemy, is no new discovery. Labor to keep alive in your breast that little spark of celestial fire called conscience; let it be your guide rather than the clamor of the hour. The silence of those who once professed regard may pain you more than the open attack, yet it also liberates you. You are not obliged to fight their battles, nor they yours. Stand upon your own ground, measure your conduct by the standard of justice and truth, and leave the rest to time and the judgment of posterity.

With every sentiment of regard for the firmness of your purpose, I remain,

Your most obedient servant,
G. Washington

text:
🇮🇳 TASL, Adani Defence, HAL and Ashok Leyland Emerge as Contenders for Coast Guard's 10 MALE Drones

WHAT
The Indian Coast Guard wants 10 Medium Altitude Long Endurance (MALE) remotely piloted aircraft. TASL (Tata Advanced Systems), Adani Defence, HAL and Ashok Leyland are described as leading contenders. Solar Industries and other interested vendors also attended the pre-bid meeting.

WHO
• Buyer: Indian Coast Guard (Aviation Wing), via the Defence Ministry
• Contenders (reported): TASL, Adani Defence, HAL, Ashok Leyland
• Also present: Solar Industries and other interested vendors

WHEN
• Programme first reported: July 2026 (RFI published around 15 July)
• Vendor responses were due 7 October 2026
• Contenders reported on: 10 October 2026
• No contract date is announced

THE PROGRAMME
• Quantity: 10 MALE drones, about ₹2,000 crore as reported
• Stage: still an RFI (Request for Information), not a final contract
• Needs: SATCOM links for beyond-line-of-sight control and real-time data to command nodes
• Area: India's 200 nm Exclusive Economic Zone and the Search and Rescue Region, up to 1,000 nm in some sectors
• Roles: maritime surveillance, search and rescue, anti-smuggling, anti-poaching and counter-drug work, including around the Andaman & Nicobar and Lakshadweep islands

WHY
Planes and helicopters can only stay up for a limited time. MALE drones can fly for more than 24 hours, so they can watch a huge ocean area continuously without risking a crew.

WHY IT MATTERS
• Coast Guard gets longer eyes over the sea, especially near Gujarat and the islands
• Indian firms are competing to build the drones, in line with Make in India
• Separate from the ₹32,000 crore plan for 87 MALE drones for the IAF, Army and Navy

WHAT WE DON'T KNOW
• Which model each firm will offer
• Whether the process moves to a formal RFP, and when
• The final value and delivery schedule

text:
Kalyani Cast-Tech Ltd is a specialised manufacturer of cargo containers & castings, with a growing integrated logistics platform. It focuses on non-commodity products tailored to Indian Railways (IR) constraints rather than pure ISO dry boxes. FY26 revenue was ~₹150–152 Cr (+~8% YoY) with PAT ~₹17 Cr (+~20%), high ROCE (~28%), and a near debt-free balance sheet. Market cap is ~₹800 Cr at ~₹1,115 (TTM P/E ~47–54x).

Competitive Advantages

Founder-led innovation is the key differentiator. CMD Naresh Kumar (IIT Madras, ex-IRSME with 17 years including senior roles at CONCOR and a major wagon/coach unit) holds more than five patents. Multiple company & industry sources state the firm holds four patents in container manufacturing. He is widely recognised as the pioneer (“father of multi-stack trains”) of the Double Stack Dwarf Container (DSDC) concept.

Dwarf Container advantages (the flagship IP):
•Lower height (~1930 mm / 6’4”) and wider (2600 mm) design allows double-stacking under standard overhead electrification on most/all IR routes, something standard ISO double-stack cannot do outside limited corridors (mainly Western DFC).
•Delivers ~67% higher volume when double-stacked versus single ISO, higher payload capacity (e.g., ~71 tonnes combined vs ~40 tonnes for typical ISO), and 20–50% lower unit transport costs for light/medium-density cargo.
•Enables capture of higher-value or lower-density freight (petrochemicals, FMCG, plastics, etc.) from road to rail. IR has issued policy circulars for DSDC operations and offered haulage discounts; commercial services have run since 2018 (e.g., from ports like JNPT).

Supporting proprietary elements include special composite/FRP flooring (lighter and thinner than traditional, claimed as a first-in-world application for this use) & custom corner castings suited to the wider dwarf design.

Hard-to-replicate advantages:
•Only Indian foundry approved by Lloyd’s Register UK for container corner fittings (a critical structural/safety component under international rules). This is a meaningful barrier.
•RDSO Class A foundry status and Indian Register of Shipping approvals for containers.
•Deep institutional relationships & regulatory know-how from the founder’s IR career, which facilitated design clearances, trials, and commercialisation.
•In-house design-to-manufacture capability for custom solutions (foldable containers, stainless-steel bulk containers for salt/steel products, cuboid containers for LTL/parcel cargo, etc.). Recent developments include stainless-steel salt containers (RDSO-advised trials) and a partnership for IceBattery reefer technology.
•Emerging vertical integration: specialised containers + new wagon designs (with Ministry/RDSO in-principle approvals) + Gati Shakti terminal + ICD in Kutch, Gujarat (near ports). This can create captive demand and cost advantages.

These elements create a practical moat in specialised/non-commoditised containers. The combination of design IP, regulatory approvals, first-mover status & relationships provides differentiation & supports higher margins versus generic assemblers. The co has already manufactured thousands of containers and driven meaningful import substitution.

Valuation Context
Tailwinds include IR’s freight modernisation & double-stack push, rising containerised traffic & the ₹10k Cr govt scheme for container manufacturing (we produce a tiny fraction of global/Chinese output). Gujarat capacity ramp (containers operational, terminal inaugurated, wagons targeted H2 FY27) plus specialised products can drive operating leverage.

At ~50x TTM earnings, the valuation prices in continued growth. Upside depends on successful wagon/terminal ramp, higher specialised-container mix & utilisation. 

Recent periods show moderation consistent with expansion & make-to-order dynamics.

Key Risks
Execution risk on large relative capex & RDSO/wagon approvals; competition as policy incentives attract more players etc.,

text:
Timepass talk on Sunday

1. Unimech - Hyper growth aspirations with complications

Unimech is a Bengaluru-based integrated precision-engineering company. It manufactures aero tooling, ground-support equipment, precision components, engineered metallic bellows and complex assemblies for aerospace, defence, energy, semiconductor and industrial sectors.

As on June 30, 2026, the company operated five manufacturing facilities, equipped with over 155+ CNC machines that are operating at ~60% utilisation, providing headroom for growth without proportionate capex in the near term.

Differentiated niche: Unimech is a qualified-SKU compounder (6,300+ SKUs, 41 customers, 96% exports) in aero tooling and precision parts. It has captured only 25–40% of the ~1,500 tools per engine programme, so existing programmes still offer room to grow.

Multiple vectors beyond tooling: LEAP engine stands (~120 shipped), Lam Research (31+ parts qualified, ₹1–1.2bn by FY29), an ASML opportunity ($50–70mn over 3–4 years), FACC ($7.5mn) and nuclear (NPCIL) all add to the tooling base.

The ₹1000cr FY29 target (50%+ CAGR): Although nothing is guaranteed, company expects, tooling ₹450–500cr + precision ₹250–260cr + Hobel ₹150–180cr + Kanoo JV ₹80–100cr sums to ₹930–104cr. Hitting the low end of every bucket gives ~₹9.3bn, so the target needs near-full delivery on all four, including two unproven ones.

Hobel is a pricey bet: Hobel was bought for ₹450bn in cash, against FY29 revenue of ₹170–200bn (~2.5x sales). Its largest customer is ~70% of revenue, and AS9100 isn’t due until April 2027, so payback depends on customer diversification and data-centre genset demand.

Margin and working capital: EBITDA is guided down from ~36% to ~32%, which management attributes to R&D and a mix shift to precision and nuclear. Those same segments carry 220–400 working capital days versus ~100–110 for tooling. A blended 170–180 days by FY29 looks hard to reconcile with that mix.

Nuclear is the swing factor: The ₹87cr refurbishment order and ~4 new tenders in 4–6 months give a visible ramp (₹38–40cr in FY27, ~₹100cr by FY29). Management itself treats ₹100cr as a ceiling because of low margins and a 350–400 day cycle, so it adds revenue but dilutes returns.

Execution and balance-sheet risks: The Saudi JV needs ~$30mn of capex, with a Feb–Mar 2027 commissioning date and local approvals still pending. On the other side, 60% CNC utilisation gives capex-light headroom. The key tracking metrics are asset turnover toward 2.5x, working capital days, and order inflow beyond the ₹280cr book (₹180cr Unimech, ₹100cr Hobel).

2. GMM Pfaudler – An infusion of B-positive blood!
Credits: Artha Vichaar Capital

GMM Pfaudler was incorporated as Gujarat Machinery Manufacturers Limited (GMM) in 1962 and got its present name in 1987 after acquisition of 40% stake by Phaudler Inc.. GMM Pfaudler is a diversified global engineering company with a heritage of more than 140 years. The Company brings together strong engineering capabilities, a cost-efficient global manufacturing footprint, and deep process know-how to help customers improve performance, reliability, and efficiency in process industries worldwide.

With 20 manufacturing facilities across four continents and a strong local presence, the Company operates through four distinct global divisions: Corrosion-Resistant Technologies (CRT), Process Performance Technologies (PPT), Heavy Engineering Technologies (HET), and Process System Technologies (PST), to serve customers worldwide.

Record order book: The backlog is ₹2,289 Cr, and order intake is ~₹1,000 Cr a quarter. Orders are forecast to rise from ₹3,714 Cr (FY26) to ₹5,540 Cr by FY29E, taking revenue from ₹3,524 Cr to ₹5,155 Cr (~13% CAGR). The plants have room, so no new glass-lined capex is needed.

Pharma is the main growth engine: Indian CDMOs and CMOs are on a capex upcycle, and US onshoring adds more demand. GMM holds over half of Indian glass-lined demand and ~40% globally, and pharma buyers rarely switch because the vendor is written into regulatory filings. Q1 FY27 orders were up 23% in CRT and 64% in PPT.

Demand is diversifying beyond chemicals: Chemicals fell from 58% to 35% of orders. Nuclear (₹130 Cr of NPCIL orders, India going from ~9 GW to ~22 GW by FY32), defence acid-recovery (a EUR 33.7m order, with USD 20–30m a year targeted) and mining (SEMCO) now take 42% of orders. A chemical capex recovery from FY28 would be pure upside.

Margin expansion from 11.4% to 15%: EBITDA is forecast to rise from ₹403 Cr to ₹772 Cr by FY29E. The drivers are operating leverage on payroll (29% to 25% of revenue), ~₹45 Cr a year of German restructuring savings, no repeat of FY26’s loss-contract provisions, and partial recovery in glass-lined pricing.

Below-EBITDA repair is the biggest profit lever: The tax rate should fall from 49% toward 30% as the loss-making entity structure is simplified. Finance cost should fall from ₹123 Cr to ~₹58 Cr through debt repayment and refinancing at 6–7% instead of ~9.9%. Together these add ~₹143 Cr to FY29E profit.

Earnings and returns compound: Adjusted EPS goes from ₹20 to ₹90 by FY29E and ROCE from 12.8% to 22.4%. Net debt turns to net cash by FY29E (₹354 Cr of net debt now), and free cash flow recovers to ~₹270 Cr.

3. Pitti Engineering - Everything inside the motor, under one roof

Pitti makes the metal parts that go inside electric motors and generators. These are the laminations (thin steel sheets stacked to form the motor core), castings (moulded metal housings) and machined parts (castings finished to exact sizes), plus shafts and full assemblies. Customers include Cummins, Marathon, Nidec, ABB, CG, Siemens etc.

Selling more: Lamination volumes were ~19,200 tons in Q1 (+19%), and Management raised the FY27 target to 82,000 tons from 78,000 tons.

Extra space already built: A ₹150 Cr expansion has just started operating. It lifts the sheet-metal (lamination) capacity to 108,000 tons a year, and also adds casting and machining capacity. Sheet-metal utilisation is 73% (up from 70%), machining is 86% (up from 82%) and casting and fabrication is 72%.

At the 80% utilisation management considers efficient, there is room for only about 8,000 tons more, which is why the next expansion is already planned.

Moving to higher-value products: Instead of selling only loose laminations, Pitti now sells finished rotor-shaft and stator assemblies that combine lamination, casting and machining. These assemblies grew about 37% in volume, against about 16% for loose laminations. The growth comes from data centres, mining, off-highway vehicles, wind power and special industrial uses. EBITDA per ton is expected to be more than double for these higher value products!

Casting and machining is the fastest-growing part: Casting capacity is now 24,000 tons, and the FY27 casting target goes up to about 17,000 tons from 16,000. Machined parts are growing over 50%, because customers want a finished part, not a raw casting. Machining is limited by how fast new machines arrive, not by orders. The ₹290 Cr project will take machining capacity to about 1.08 million machine hours, in steps over the coming quarters.

Many industries and a global shift to India: Traction motors and railways revenue share stands at 28%, power generation 15%, industrial and commercial 12%, mining and oil & gas 10% (doubled from 5%), special motors 9%, data centres 5%, renewables 3% and others 17%. Companies are moving production from China and Europe to India because of high European energy and labour costs. Some of what Pitti supplies to global companies’ Indian plants is later exported, which management calls indirect exports. North American railway modernisation is another source of demand. Management is cautious about data centres, saying AI-related spending may not last, so it is not building capacity far ahead for them.

Exports should recover: Exports were flat at about ₹139 Cr (against about ₹137 Cr last year), while domestic sales grew 23%. Management expects direct exports to rise each quarter from Q2 to Q4 as the new capacity ramps up.

Profits should grow faster than sales: The Q1 adjusted EBITDA margin was 16.8%, held back because staff and costs for the new plants are already in place while volumes have not yet caught up. Management guides FY27 EBITDA of about ₹370 Cr. Next year it expects turnover above ₹2,500 Cr at a 17–17.2% margin, assuming 90,000 tons and no further lamination capacity. Within about three years it expects margins of 18–18.5%. The tax rate should be about 25% for the full year (Q1 was lower because of a one-off deferred tax effect). A state incentive of about ₹40 Cr a year is expected from next year, but not this year, and about ₹70 Cr of past incentives is still to be received in the next 9–12 months.

Size ambition: current capacity supports about ₹2,500 Cr of revenue. Adding the ₹290 Cr project and a further ₹400 Cr (a ₹200 Cr Bangalore plant and ₹200 Cr of equipment) would support ₹3,000–3,300 Cr. The Bangalore plant is not yet approved by the board.

Risks: Net debt is ₹491 Cr with more capex coming, mining and data-centre demand can reverse quickly, and the margin gains are so far only guidance.

4. The Rising Cancer Burden

Cancer remains one of the world's biggest healthcare challenges, with around 20+ million new cases reported anually. The global cancer burden is projected to rise to 35 million annual cases by 2050, driving the need for more effective and targeted treatments.

For decades, cancer treatment has largely relied on chemotherapy, radiation and surgery. Chemotherapy works by killing rapidly dividing cells, including cancer cells, but it can also damage healthy cells, leading to side effects such as hair loss, fatigue and nausea. While these treatments have saved millions of lives, treating cancer effectively without causing significant damage to the rest of the body has remained a major challenge. 

Targeted therapies and immunotherapy have improved treatment outcomes, but not every patient responds, and cancers can eventually develop resistance.

Antibody-Drug Conjugates (ADCs) are changing the dynamics by combining the targeting ability of antibodies with the cancer-killing power of chemotherapy.

Think of them as guided missiles: the antibody identifies specific proteins on cancer cells and delivers a potent drug payload more directly to the tumour, potentially reducing damage to healthy cells. The technology is evolving rapidly, with future growth driven by new targets, more effective payloads, better linkers and the development of ADCs for additional cancer types and earlier stages of treatment.

The next frontier includes combination therapies and next-generation ADC designs, making this an exciting area of innovation for the pharmaceutical industry. However, ADCs are not side-effect-free, and their success depends on the cancer type, target and individual patient.

The ADC field reached a defining inflection point in 2025. According to the Beacon ADC database maintained by Hanson Wade, a total of 2,334 distinct antibody-based drug conjugates were tracked globally as of January 5, 2026, representing a 20% YoY increase in traditional ADCs and an extraordinary 88% YoY increase in novel ADC formats.

Most strikingly, 130 new ADC candidates progressed into clinical development in 2025, a 49% increase over the prior year and the highest single-year clinical entry figure ever recorded.

Among Indian CDMO names, Piramal Pharma, Cohance Lifesciences, Anthem Biosciences, Sai Life, Shilpa Medicare, Syngene, and Laurus Labs have established or are building capabilities linked to ADCs in one form or another.

5. Gravita India

Gravita India is facing near-term execution challenges as geopolitical disruptions have affected scrap availability. Management explained that 15–20% of its scrap imports came from the Gulf region, with shipments from other countries also affected by transit disruptions. Lead volumes have suffered, and management cautioned that Q2 FY27 could also see an impact, although it expects to protect EBITDA margins through better realisations and product mix. Q1 FY27 EBITDA per tonne stood at ₹24,181 for lead, ₹25,175 for aluminium, ₹10,197 for plastic and ₹55,151 for copper. Meanwhile, copper capacity utilisation remains around 50%, and elevated working capital is another monitorable.

All of this has led to a cooling off in valuations. At current levels, the stock is trading below its 5-year median valuations.

However, the near-term story, including the remainder of FY27, appears challenging. It’s not a bargain yet, but valuations are certainly looking more reasonable.

The longer-term opportunity remains meaningful. Gravita's acquisition of Rashtriya Metal Industries (RMIL) expands its presence in copper and copper alloys, while its new 29,400-tonne copper recycling facility and plans to double copper capacity to around 60,000 tonnes over three years provide additional growth avenues. Management targets copper EBITDA per tonne of ₹70,000–75,000 over the next 2–3 years, supported by debottlenecking, better procurement and integration.

With total installed capacity targeted to rise from 4.97 lakh tonnes to over 8 lakh tonnes by FY29, Gravita has room to scale, provided scrap sourcing normalises, utilisation improves and returns on invested capital strengthen. Management's 25–30% annual PAT growth aspiration is encouraging, but execution remains key.

Could Gravita offer a more attractive opportunity post Q2 results? We’ll have to wait and watch!

That's all for this edition. Have a great Sunday!

In some tales:  Two men swear brotherhood before a cross. One betrays the other. Misfortune follows the oath-breaker. The cross becomes a witness before God.  The idea comes from the ancient belief that sacred objects could not be deceived.  Crosses and the Ruins of Ani  Since you've often asked about Ani, several local legends developed after the city's abandonment.  One legend claims that:  The crosses remained guarding the churches long after the people left.  Another says:  Angels continued to pray in the ruined sanctuaries where crosses still stood.  Some travelers in later centuries reported hearing stories that lights appeared among ruined churches at night. Historians treat these as local folklore, not documented supernatural events.  The Cemetery Crosses  Perhaps the darkest Armenian cross folklore concerns graveyard crosses.  In folk belief:  A neglected grave might produce restless dreams. A fallen cross should be restored. Stealing stone from a grave marker invited misfortune. Spirits remained peaceful when their cross was maintained.  Many such beliefs survived in rural communities well into modern times.  Crosses Against the Al  One particularly ancient Armenian tradition involved the Al, a feared supernatural being from Armenian folklore.  The Al was blamed for:  Night attacks Illness around childbirth Unexplained weakness  People sometimes placed crosses, prayers, or blessed objects near mothers and infants as protection.  This reflects the blending of older Armenian supernatural beliefs with Christian symbols.  The Dark Winter Crosses  In old mountain regions there were tales of lonely crosses standing in snowfields.  The stories often say:  Wolves would not pass the shadow of a blessed cross. Travelers trapped in blizzards found shelter after praying before one. Spirits of the wilderness could not cross ground marked by it.  These legends are especially atmospheric around places like the highlands near Ani, where medieval churches and khachkars stand against harsh winter landscapes.  A Gothic Armenian Folklore Image  Imagine a moonlit winter night outside the walls of Ani. Snow covers the ruined streets. A solitary khachkar leans beside a forgotten path. Wind moves through the empty churches. Villagers once whispered that no spirit could pass that stone, because although the city had died, the ancient cross remained awake, keeping watch over the lost capital until dawn.  That image is not a historical fact, but it captures the mood of many Armenian folk stories in which ancient crosses are less symbols of death than silent guardians standing between the living world and the unknown.    Ani Sun Magazine X Protection Against Evil  Yes. There are a few real Armenian monastery legends that were actually recorded and passed down around specific monasteries. They are legends, not verified historical events, but they are genuine traditions attached to real places.  Geghard Monastery and the Invisible Army  One of the darker legends surrounds Geghard Monastery, the famous cave monastery that once housed the relic known as the Holy Lance, the spear believed in Armenian tradition to have pierced Christ's side. The monastery's very name, "Geghard," means "spear."  A later Armenian legend says that when the conqueror Tamerlane sought to seize the relic, his soldiers entered the monastery and encountered an invisible heavenly army. Some were said to be struck blind, others paralyzed with fear, forcing the invaders to retreat.  The story reflects a common Armenian theme: sacred monasteries protected not by earthly soldiers, but by unseen divine guardians.  The Holy Spring Beneath the Mountain  Before Christianity, the site of Geghard Monastery was associated with a sacred cave spring. When Christianity arrived, the monastery was founded around that ancient holy place. Traditions grew up around the spring, whose waters were believed to possess healing powers.  Some local stories claimed the spring never truly slept and that the mountain itself remembered the prayers spoken there.  The Whispering Stone Chambers  A particularly eerie tradition attached to Geghard concerns its acoustics.  The monastery contains chambers carved directly into solid rock. According to local legend, the stone walls remember every prayer ever spoken within them. The tale arose because chants echo for an unusually long time in the carved halls.  A visitor standing alone in the darkened chambers can easily understand how such a legend developed.  Tatev's Shaking Pillar  At Tatev Monastery stands the famous Gavazan, or "staff," a stone column constructed in the 10th century.  Historically, it functioned as an architectural and warning feature. Over time, legends developed that the pillar moved when danger approached or when hostile forces neared the monastery. The monastery itself became associated with miraculous protection during periods of invasion.  For medieval villagers, a moving stone column overlooking a deep gorge must have felt deeply uncanny.  The Lost Monasteries of Ani  Among the ruins of Ani, many churches and monastic buildings stand abandoned today.  Travelers in later centuries recorded local stories that lights appeared among the ruins at night, while some guides spoke of hearing distant bells from churches where no monks remained. These are folk traditions rather than documented medieval accounts, but they became part of the atmosphere surrounding the "City of 1,001 Churches."
