FACT-CHECK–NO-SPIN
PART 1 OF 4 — TRUMP, THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY, AND THE COMMUNISM ACCUSATION

October 11, 2026 | Examination of Trump's October 10 remarks
On October 10, President Donald Trump spoke with reporters at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, after returning from a political rally in Tennessee.

He argued that the Democratic Party should abandon its current name because, in his characterization, it has become a combination of socialists and communists.

He also used the derogatory nickname “Dumocrat.”

What, precisely, is he alleging?

That the Democratic Party is no longer meaningfully democratic, that socialist and communist factions have overtaken it, and that its existing political identity is misleading.

There are real ideological developments behind parts of this claim.

However, the evidence does not establish the sweeping transformation Trump describes.

1. THE ORIGINAL SOURCE

The remarks occurred during an approximately eight-minute press exchange at Joint Base Andrews.

White House correspondent Katherine Doyle's contemporaneous pool report confirms that Trump deplaned shortly after 8 p.m. and answered questions concerning the midterm elections, John Fetterman, Iran, Ukraine, and other topics.

The circulating clip is an excerpt of those original remarks. (i)(ii)

Trump was not making a detailed policy argument.

He offered no list of proposed communist legislation, no count of communist lawmakers, and no evidence showing that a majority of Democratic officeholders seek to establish a communist economy.

His argument was made through political labeling and ridicule.

That distinction matters.

2. THIS IS NOT A NEW ACCUSATION

At the Republican midterm convention on September 9, 2026, Trump repeatedly described Democratic socialists as communists.

He warned that a Democratic congressional majority could become controlled by a communist faction.

https://t.co/UpBoRUyga1 examined those claims on September 10 and found that he was conflating different ideological traditions and overstating the representation of democratic socialists among congressional candidates.

Trump used the word communist or communism fifteen times during that convention address. (iii)

His October 10 remarks therefore continue an established public campaign message.

That conclusion concerns the documented repetition of his rhetoric, not an assumption about his private motivations.

3. WHAT IS THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY'S ACTUAL PLATFORM?

The Democratic National Committee's 2024 platform is a formal statement of the party's adopted national positions.

It supports private small businesses, job creation, private investment, industrial development, labor protections, existing constitutional institutions, and a combination of public programs and regulated private markets.

It calls small businesses an engine of the American economy.

The platform does not propose abolishing private enterprise, establishing a one-party communist state, or eliminating capitalism as the basis of the national economy.

It does advocate more government intervention in healthcare, taxation, infrastructure, energy, and worker protections.

Those policies can be debated on their actual merits. But intervention in a capitalist economy is not automatically communism. (iv)

The 2024 platform is also not a guarantee that every Democratic candidate in 2026 supports every provision. Candidates differ, and congressional policy is shaped by elected members and actual votes.

4. THE PARTY CONTAINS REAL IDEOLOGICAL DIVISIONS

The Democratic Party includes centrists, market-oriented liberals, traditional progressives, labor-oriented reformers, and democratic socialists.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries has explicitly distinguished his positions from those of the Democratic Socialists of America.

In August 2026, he rejected the DSA's agenda concerning abolishing the Senate, defunding police, and immigration policy.

He simultaneously acknowledged that candidates elected through Democratic primaries may join the Democratic congressional caucus even if they belong to its socialist wing.

That is a description of a heterogeneous electoral coalition, not an announcement that the DSA's entire program has become Democratic Party policy. (v)

5. WHY DO SOCIALISTS RUN IN DEMOCRATIC PRIMARIES?

The DSA itself provides an explanation.

Its July 2026 organizational material acknowledges that America's electoral system strongly favors the two major parties.

Rather than always running separate third-party candidates, socialist organizations frequently seek nominations on the Democratic ballot line.

The DSA also openly criticizes the Democratic Party and seeks to build an independent working-class political movement.

A socialist candidate using the Democratic ballot line is not, by itself, evidence that every other Democratic candidate agrees with that person's ideology. (vi)

6. HOW MUCH ELECTORAL REACH DOES THE DSA ACTUALLY HAVE?

A Brookings Institution analysis examined 64 DSA-endorsed congressional candidates in 2026.

As of August 12, 19 had won Democratic primaries, with some outcomes still unresolved.

Those totals count endorsements, not necessarily verified DSA membership.

The research found meaningful gains for socialist-aligned candidates but limited reach relative to the broader congressional election landscape. (vii)

That finding does not mean a small ideological faction can never exercise legislative leverage.

In a closely divided chamber, a relatively small bloc can influence negotiations, procedural votes, or whether proposed legislation has enough support.

But possible leverage is not equivalent to proven control of Congress.

That requires examining actual caucus membership, negotiations, leadership decisions, and roll-call votes.

7. IS THE WORD “DEMOCRAT” INACCURATE?

The organization is formally named the Democratic Party.

Political party names are historical institutional identifiers. They do not have to function as complete philosophical definitions of every member or policy.

A party can contain internal disagreements and still retain its legal and political name.

Whether its actions fulfill democratic principles is a separate question involving elections, representative institutions, constitutional rights, and governing conduct.

Calling it the “Dumocrat” Party supplies no evidence about those matters.

It is an insult, not a constitutional or economic analysis.

PART 1 CONCLUSION

Trump's statement refers to a real socialist movement operating within Democratic electoral politics.

But identifying that movement does not establish that the Democratic Party as a whole has become communist.

The accurate questions are:

Which candidates support socialism?

What specific policies do they advocate?

How much legislative power do they possess?

Which proposals are actually supported by Democratic congressional leadership?

And which of those proposals would survive constitutional and legislative scrutiny?

Those questions can be investigated.

The derogatory nickname cannot answer them.

text:
It’s been a while ago but Brothers Karamazov ended up on my list after an upperclassman said Hemingway considered it the perfect novel. My takeaway is that the psychic suffering is real, precisely because “truth” in many important ways is unknowable, uncertain, or delayed. The denouement offers an opportunity for some moral teaching, but for me it’s mostly to highlight the fog itself.

There is a popular conversation about the fuzzy-tech divide at Stanford, and when it comes to the great upheavals of the 20th century, history scores one for the techies for being on the “right” side of history, focusing on the problems that could be solved objectively and being generally suspicious of the new -isms that promised to correct the ills a nation faced. America took in Einstein and Einstein pushed for the bomb that almost arrived in time to stop fascism and did stop virtually all unilateral border aggression. What could be more techy than that? That’s nation-state peace.

But what does the scientific community, having been justified for all its reactionary politics, actually envision about the future of society, other than the continual integration of new technologies? As you asked, who is writing novels concerning the nation’s soul in a post-modern world where any narrative being sold is distrusted? The legacy we are left with after the -isms is skepticism. We cannot know, and to try and convince everybody of the one true path is not so wrong as it is futile. Some national coherence died in the 20th century, and we’ve been splintering everyone’s perception of reality with each new advancement of communication technology.

And still, in our fog, we have three ways to engage with the world: impulsively, analytically, or humanistically. The struggle Dostoevsky had in a post-Kantian world is the same struggle we have today. There is no general resolution.

I have not read Life and Fate. From your description, it appears to deal less with the fog than the horror. But I think it’s the fog that gives national discourse the special flavor it has today.

This might have been made with AI, but situations like this are common in construction for one reason.

If you have been to the Mende area of Lagos, Maryland, you might see some examples.

In this area, I saw someone's building undergoing underpinning because it was sinking.

The main reason for this sinking is usually a poor foundation, which can happen for various reasons.

1. It might have been due to the wrong type of foundation adopted (in most cases in zones like that Mende Arowojobe side, it is advisable, depending on what your soil investigation comes out with, to use a pile foundation), but some clients go with raft foundations anyway, hoping that somehow the acclaimed engineer would be able to offer a workable solution; then, before you know it, the building starts sinking after completion.

2. Poorly constructed foundation. Sometimes, although piles were used, they were poorly done or poorly tested before loading. So, in zones like that, the foundation stage of construction is not where you cut costs. It is where you ensure you get the best service.

text:
Dear Michael, as the cliche goes, you are entitled to your own opinion but not your own facts. What you write here is somewhat misleading. 

Had it not been for the intervention of Boris Johnson and the opposition of influential figures in Washington, including Victoria Nuland, Ukraine might have had a genuine opportunity to end this catastrophic war in the spring of 2022, before the destruction and loss of life reached their present proportions.

The possibility of a negotiated settlement was not imaginary. Ukrainian and Russian negotiators had made substantial progress in Istanbul. Ukraine had indicated its willingness to accept permanent neutrality in exchange for binding international security guarantees. Questions concerning Crimea and Donbas could potentially have been addressed through separate negotiations.

Yet rather than energetically pursuing this diplomatic opening, Western governments increasingly embraced the prospect of confronting and weakening Russia through continued Ukrainian resistance. Johnson’s intervention in Kyiv in April 2022 reflected that approach, encouraging Zelensky to resist Putin rather than pursue an accommodation.

Nor was Istanbul the first missed opportunity. In December 2021, Russia had demanded negotiations over NATO enlargement and European security arrangements. Washington rejected Moscow’s demand for a veto over Ukrainian NATO membership, although it offered discussions on other security issues. Whether a more imaginative diplomatic response could have averted the invasion remains an important and insufficiently examined question.

None of this absolves Putin of responsibility for invading Ukraine. But acknowledging Russia’s responsibility does not absolve Western governments of responsibility for their own decisions, particularly when those decisions may have narrowed opportunities for peace.

The tragedy is that diplomacy was treated increasingly as an obstacle to military objectives rather than as the indispensable means of ending the slaughter.

We cannot know whether the Istanbul negotiations would ultimately have succeeded. But the possibility that a negotiated settlement might have spared Ukraine years of devastation deserves serious scrutiny, not dismissal. The human cost of failing to secure peace has been staggering, and the question of whether that cost was avoidable remains one of the most consequential questions of this war.

text:
At some point, we will have to blame Mearsheimer, Sachs, and their fellow travelers for much more than just peddling wrong explanations and misleading people. These guys have influence in policy circles, their words have policy consequences. They are partly responsible for policies that are based on their explanations. 

The U.S. has now said no NATO membership for Ukraine — and the Russians didn’t even bother to thank it. 

The U.S. has pursued deescalation — and the Kremlin merely escalated in return. 

The U.S. has offered lucrative deals to Moscow — and the Russians have not offered anything at all.

The U.S. denigrated and pressured Zelenskyy multiple times — and the Kremlin just clapped. 

The U.S. pulled Putin out of increasing international isolation by rolling out the red carpet for him in Alaska — and the Kremlin just used “the spirit of Alaska” to support its demands for Ukraine to capitulate. 

The Russians still demand all of Donbas just to start talking. 

And the reason for all these failure is rather simple: the U.S. keeps offering things that should appeal to the Russians under the Mearsheimer/Sachs explanation of the war but don’t. 

Because their explanation is fundamentally and irretrievably wrong. 

The moment you ditch the Mearshemer/Sachs framework, everything will immediately fall into place and you will understand why all these initiatives never had any chance of success. 

Putin wants to subjugate Ukraine. 

That’s the starting point. From this, it follows that he does not want it in NATO. It follows that he does not want it to have an army. It follows that he does not want it to have an independent government.

But, you might say, this is consistent with the other framework too. It is. But the imperialist explanation also tells you why Putin is fixated on territories, why he insists on taking Donbas, and why no economic and security concessions work on him. It tells you why all these talks will never work. 

Mearsheimer is reduced to blubbering utter gibberish when confronted with that reality. After denying expansionist motives for years, he had to bow to reality and so began to claim — without a shred of evidence — that the territorial demands came only after the invasion. That’s despite the Kremlin officially annexing Donetsk and Luhansk even before the invasion, and Putin ceaselessly talking about subjugation and territory.

text:
will have none of it. The cross does not need a religious co-signer.
“by whom the world is crucified unto me,”
Paul now explains what the cross has done to his relationship with the world: “by whom the world is crucified unto me.” The world here is not the physical creation itself, nor does Paul mean Christians must cease caring about people. God made creation, and believers are commanded to do good unto all men. The world in this moral sense is the present system organized apart from God—its values, ambitions, pride, approval, lusts, honours, and rebellion. First John 2:16 identifies “the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life.”
Through Christ’s cross, Paul sees that system under judgment. Something crucified has lost its rightful claim upon him. The world still exists, still advertises, still pressures, still threatens, and still offers applause, but the cross has exposed what it is worth compared with Christ. Philippians 3:8 says Paul counted all things “but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord.” Calvary rearranged his values.
This is particularly significant after verse 12, where the legalizers were altering their message to avoid persecution. They cared about what the religious world thought. Paul sees that very world as crucified. A dead world cannot offer enough applause to compensate for betraying a living Christ. Once the world’s approval loses ultimate value, persecution loses some of its bargaining power.
This does not mean believers become irresponsible hermits. Paul travelled through cities, worked with his hands, taught publicly, used Roman citizenship, and interacted with unbelievers. Separation is moral and spiritual, not theatrical withdrawal from human society. The Christian lives in the world without letting the world supply his identity, doctrine, morality, or final standard.
“and I unto the world.”
The verse finishes with the other side of crucifixion: “and I unto the world.” Not only is the world crucified to Paul; Paul is crucified to the world. The relationship has been broken in both directions. The world no longer occupies the throne in Paul’s affections, and Paul no longer expects the world to crown him.
This echoes Galatians 2:20: “I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me.” The cross changes identity and allegiance. The believer is not physically dead, but the old basis of life—self, worldly approval, fleshly boasting—stands beneath Calvary’s judgment. Romans 6:6 similarly says, “our old man is crucified with him.”
Being crucified unto the world therefore means accepting the loss of its approval when faithfulness requires it. A man nailed to a cross is not climbing down to attend an awards banquet. The Christian who must constantly be admired by the world will eventually be tempted to edit whatever part of Christianity the world finds offensive. Paul had already chosen his side.
Yet this crucifixion is liberty, not misery. The believer freed from worldly approval can finally serve Christ without checking the cultural weather every morning. He does not need the world to certify his faith, reward his obedience, or applaud his doctrine. The cross has already settled where his glory belongs.

text:
🔘 What We Defend, What We Fight For – What This Is All About

In Warsaw in 2017, beside the monument to the Uprising, Donald Trump said: "Our values will prevail." He listed them – faith and family, symphonies, innovation, the rule of law, free speech, the dignity of every life, liberty, sovereignty. A good list. But a list is not a framework.

The Polish historian Feliks Koneczny offered one. A civilization, he said, is a method of organizing collective life – and no society can live by two incompatible methods at once. Poland, for him, was the eastern outpost of Latin civilization: Greece, Rome, and Western Christianity.

That civilization was built in layers.

🔘 From the Greeks

Truth, goodness, beauty. Spiritual goods above material ones – that is the Latin order of things.

Science. Reason, evidence, open to criticism, open to new methods. Freedom of inquiry, limited only by the protection of human beings. Copernicus studied in Kraków. Marie Curie was born in Warsaw.

🔘 From Rome

Law. Justice is giving each person their due. No retroactive laws. No one forced to incriminate himself. Poland guaranteed – long before England’s Habeas Corpus – no imprisonment without a court judgment.

Two spheres. Public and private are distinct. The state is not the ruler’s property, and governing a territory does not mean owning everything in it. Law is subject to ethics – passing a statute does not make it right.

Property. A basic right, protected against the state itself. Koneczny judged every civilization by three things: family, property, inheritance. In the Latin model, all three protect the person against an all-powerful state.

🔘 From Christianity

The Ten Commandments. The foundation of personal and public morality.

Universalism. No one is above moral judgment – not by birth, not by rank. A Polish scholar argued before a church council that pagan peoples had the right to their own states and could not be converted by the sword.

The person. Each person answers for his own acts. No collective guilt, no herd. Self-reliance is a virtue. John Paul II built his philosophy on this.

Dignity. Every human life has it, regardless of age, health, or ability.

The family. Monogamous marriage. Parents and children above the clan.

Time. Not to be wasted. A bond between generations – memory of the past, responsibility for the future.

Self-government. Society organizes itself from the bottom up, and rulers and ruled answer to the same morals. "Nothing about us without us." Ten million Poles lived it in Solidarity.

Defense. A duty of citizens, not a job for hired soldiers.

Subsidiarity. The higher level does only what the lower ones cannot – the family first, then the town, then the region.

The nation. A spiritual and cultural community held together by allegiance, not blood. "Ruthenian by origin, Polish by nation," as one Renaissance writer described himself.

🔘 The Modern Layer

Liberty – yours ends where another’s rights begin. "For our freedom and yours" – a Polish motto.

Free speech – full, won against censors, kept alive under Communism by émigré and underground presses.

Religious toleration – the state does not impose a faith. While Europe burned heretics, Poland was a state without stakes. Its king: "I am not the king of your consciences." This fits with the Commandments: conscience binds the person; the state compels only what law may compel.

Pluralism – different faiths and ways of life under one law. Catholics, Orthodox, Protestants, Jews and Armenians shared the old Commonwealth.

Excellence – not just living alongside each other, but learning from the best.

🔘 So

Only when we know what these values are and where they come from can we argue about them seriously. Are they sound? Do they hold together, or pull apart? Are they worth defending?

Trump said our values will prevail. They will – if we can still name them. A civilization that cannot say what it stands for has already started to lose it.

Grok:

“Zero. No state requires you to physically travel there for a birth or marriage certificate — every one of the fifty lets you order by mail, and nearly all offer online ordering too, either through the state’s own portal or a vendor like VitalChek.
The catch is that marriage records live at the county level in about a dozen states — Arizona, Illinois, Minnesota, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Texas, and others — so you’re mailing to a specific county clerk, not a state office. And a few states have quirks: California went mail-only for marriage records in July 2026, and some states restrict who can get a certified copy, like Georgia, which limits marriage certificates to the two spouses.

text:
Little treat for Sunday 7am club. I have been trying to kill time this weekend while I wait for Monday morning, so I listened to Andrew’s interviews again. It’s been such a busy week, and in all the overexcitement, I think some bullish points may have been forgotten about. So, I’ve put together a recap of @asjwebley’s interviews from the past week. It doesn’t capture everything, but here are some of the points I found particularly useful and exciting for SWC and MORE.

@OneChairPod

- Many institutional investors would like to put £/$10m+ into MORE, but they can’t get involved at this stage. There is capital waiting in the wings as MORE scales.
- Some of the institutional investors interested in MORE have also had their interest piqued by SWC ordinary shares. They understand the synergy.
- Andrew thinks the IPO will be a roughly 50/50 split between retail and institutional capital.
- If he could choose, he would prefer more retail than institutional participation. He would like retail investors to benefit from an attractive IPO offer, rather than having to buy shares later from an institution that only took part to flip them.
- He thinks large lump sums will follow from institutions in the months to come.
- Discussed the importance of preferred shares in improving Bitcoin per share in all market conditions. Selling common equity only works in a buoyant market.
- Andrew has been able to revisit institutional investors he has been speaking to over the past 12–18 months to explain how MORE can benefit the SWC share price, even if they’re not interested in MORE itself. He said this strategy has definitely worked so far in terms of increasing interest in SWC.
- He believes we have achieved a lot in a tough market, and he is clearly excited about what could be achieved in a bull market (the term “mind-blowing” was used).
- The company looks at a lot of acquisition opportunities, not necessarily just UK-based companies. Web design and tech are the main areas of focus, and the business needs to be cash-generating. In the long term, he would like to support something in the Bitcoin space.
- The company name and the possibility of rebranding were discussed. Andrew doesn’t know the right answer and is attached to the name and the history associated with it. He feels it is a recognised name and brand that means something to a lot of people. He acknowledges the merit in the idea that the company name should possibly reflect what the company will become over the next 5+ years.

@TNorth / @AdamBLiv

- Andrew has observed STRC and SATA closely since they were established, and he believes MORE will take us to the next level.
- Capital raising can be counterintuitive. Conversely, it’s easier to raise capital in a bull market when Bitcoin and shares are more expensive.
- Andrew and Adam discussed how the purchase price of Bitcoin isn’t the most important thing. For example, “expensive” Bitcoin purchased using equity sold at a high mNAV is better for shareholders than cheap Bitcoin purchased at a low mNAV.
- The UK capital market was acknowledged to be much smaller than the US market, but it is very focused on income, which is great for MORE. Andrew mentioned that the fact we have raised in excess of £250m is all the more impressive when viewed through this lens.
- Daily dividends aren’t a priority at present, but this could be revisited when MORE reaches £50–100m.
- An institution that may or may not be supporting the IPO was pleasantly surprised by the investor protections in place.
- When discussing amplification, Andrew stressed the importance of total returns. He is fully aware that portfolio returns typically mean more to investors than BTC per share growth, while acknowledging that the latter is still important.
- There was a candid discussion about when it is the right time to add leverage/amplification in relation to where we are in the Bitcoin cycle. Andrew was surprised that many companies did not use leverage after the price of BTC fell. He believes companies should add leverage when things are cheap.
- He believes there will be increased demand for ordinary shares when people see MORE working.
- Adam confirmed that the community successfully badgered him into reaching out to Andrew about an interview - go 7am club!
- Andrew is hopeful of FTSE 250 qualification early next year, although he believes the December cut-off will likely be too soon. This is the key thing Andrew wants to achieve in the near term.
- He believes the next three years will be incredible for BTC.

@StephanLivera

- A detailed overview of SWC and MORE, including the domestic advantages of MORE.
- Discussed the importance of currency and FX risk, as well as dividend withholding tax considerations.
- A reminder that management execution is what ultimately makes the difference.

General/repeated points

- 35% amplification is the initial target, not necessarily the ceiling. The priority is to build trust and establish a track record first. 50% was mentioned as a potential future figure, not a committed target.
- Paying down the Coinbase facility is a priority, ensuring MORE investors hold the most senior claim. This will be hugely important when attracting institutional capital in the future.
- Andrew confirmed that @ColeMacro has been really helpful, particularly in relation to investor protections for MORE.
- A clean, easy-to-understand balance sheet is seen as vitally important.

My overall takeaway

They were all great interviews in their own right, and each offered something a bit different. The One Chair Pod was full of bull fuel, while the chat with Adam was great fun to listen to. It was also great to hear them discuss aspects of digital credit and Bitcoin treasuries that haven’t really been covered before. The interview with Stephan was very informative and gave a great breakdown of where the company is today.

text:
Before we examine Golda Meir's offer, we must understand the language she and her successors used. Israeli leaders have systematically avoided the word Palestinian — not by accident, but by design. Golda Meir herself said in 1969: There was no such thing as Palestinians. Ben-Gurion spoke of the Arabs of the Land of Israel. Netanyahu speaks of Arab Israelis and residents of the territories. Why? Because if there is no Palestinian people, there is no occupation, no displacement, no right of return. The erasure of the name is the first step toward erasing the people.

Golda Meir stood before the UN General Assembly offering a meeting with no preconditions with Ben-Gurion. But what were these conditions that were supposedly not conditions?

That the Arabs recognize Israel as it was — on 78% of Palestine — after it had expelled 1,000,000 Palestinians from their homes, after the massacres of Deir Yassin (1948), Qibya (1953), and Kafr Qasim (1956). That they sit with the butchers of their people as if nothing had happened. That they negotiate a non-aggression pact with the one who raped their land. This is not a peace offer. This is a surrender offer.

Meir said Israel was a tiny sliver of land. Yes, a tiny sliver — but a stolen sliver. The West Bank was Jordanian, Gaza was Egyptian, and Haifa, Jaffa, Lydd, and Ramla were Palestinian. Who gave Israel the right to ask Nasser and Hussein to give up land that was not Israel's?

Meir offered a meeting with no preconditions — but she had already erased the very people she claimed to want to talk to. In her mind, there was no Palestinian people to negotiate with, only Arabs who happened to live there. So what was she offering? Not peace with a people, but recognition of a state. She wanted the Arab regimes to legitimize Israel, not to address the rights of the Palestinians. How can you negotiate with someone whose existence you deny?

Then the text weeps for Meir because Shuqairy called her a Nazi. As if one harsh word equals a massacre against an entire people. As if the Arabs started the hostility. But who declared a state on land that was not theirs in 1948? Who refused the return of refugees under Resolution 194? Who built settlements on the ruins of 500 depopulated villages?

The truth the text ignores: Israel did not want real peace. It wanted recognition only. Recognition that would grant it legitimacy for its occupation, erase the refugee question, and kill any hope of return. Meir's offer mentioned no Jerusalem, no refugees, no borders. It only said: come talk. But who talks to a thief about what? About how to divide what was stolen?

Ahmad Shuqairy used the word Nazi twelve times. But was he entirely wrong? Who burned villages? Who put Palestinians in camps? Who passed laws preventing refugees from returning? Who occupied the West Bank, Gaza, the Golan, and Sinai after 1967? If Nazi is too harsh a word, then what do we call what happened to us?

The text says Meir asked for a meeting, was rebuffed, and called the name of the people who had exterminated the Jews of Europe. But Meir herself once said: There is no such thing as a Palestinian people. This is not a slip of the tongue — it is the foundation of the entire Zionist narrative. Ben-Gurion spoke of the Arabs of the Land of Israel. Netanyahu speaks of Arab Israelis and residents of the territories. They avoid the word Palestinian because naming a people means recognizing their right to self-determination, their right of return, and the injustice done to them. Meir denied our existence while demanding recognition for hers. She refused refugee return. She led a government that invaded Lebanon in 1978. So who started the violence?

This is not a racist article. This is an Israeli propaganda piece dressed in the clothes of history. It selects true facts to hide the original crime: the occupation of Palestine and the displacement of its people — a people whose very name Israel refuses to speak. It accuses the Arabs of rejection, while forgetting that the rejection was a response to injustice, and that the word Nazi — however harsh — came from a people who were being exterminated, expelled, and erased.

Real peace does not begin with an offer of a meeting without preconditions on occupied land. It begins with acknowledging the injustice, the right of return, and the fact that Palestine is not a sliver of land but the homeland of a people — a people with a name, a history, and a right to exist.

text:
On this day—October 10, 1960

Golda Meir offered the Arab states a meeting with Ben-Gurion, no conditions. The Arab answer was no and to call her a Nazi in a UN tirade.

Foreign Minister Meir stood in the UN General Assembly and said the Prime Minister was ready to sit down, in New York or anywhere else, without preconditions, to talk peace or at least a non-aggression pact. Israel was a tiny sliver of land with a waist only nine miles wide after the 1949 armistice. Still the Arabs refused to even talk peace.

Meir addressed Egypt’s Nasser, Jordan’s Hussein, and the Lebanese prime minister by name. A Western European delegate told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency it was the most reasonable proposal he had heard in a long time.

Then came the response.

Ahmad Shukairy of Saudi Arabia took the right of reply and used the word “Nazi” a dozen times. “Nazi Zionism.” A “Nazi war of aggression.” Five days later, Nasser said Israel was trying to deceive world opinion and that Egypt would never recognize the Jewish state.

Shukairy would later become the first chairman of the PLO and would draft its charter that refused a Jewish state in any borders. 

Meir had simply asked for a meeting. She was rebuffed and called the name of the people who had exterminated the Jews of Europe.

No More Compromise on National Security: Federal Government Decides to Impose Governor’s Rule and Emergency in KP

The federal government has reportedly reached an in-principle decision to impose Governor’s Rule and a state of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution of Pakistan, following repeated disagreements with the provincial government over security cooperation.

According to sources, the decision follows several rounds of negotiations and repeated requests for the KP government to cooperate with federal institutions in implementing a coordinated national security framework. The federal government maintains that the provincial administration has failed to provide the required cooperation despite multiple opportunities.

Article 232 allows the proclamation of an emergency in circumstances involving war, external aggression or internal disturbances beyond the control of a provincial government, subject to constitutional requirements. Article 234 allows the President to assume certain provincial government functions, or authorize the Governor to exercise them, when the province cannot be governed in accordance with the Constitution, subject to parliamentary oversight.

However, sources indicate that the federal government has decided to offer the provincial administration one final opportunity before proceeding with the proposed measures.

JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman has reportedly been requested to contact the KP government and persuade its leadership to cooperate with federal authorities and security institutions.

If the provincial government agrees to implement the proposed security framework and extend the necessary institutional cooperation, the decision to impose Governor’s Rule and emergency measures could be postponed.

The government’s position, according to sources, is that national security and counterterrorism efforts cannot be compromised any further.

text:
*India: Not an Inspiration...but a Warning*

*Japan, a nation decimated by two nuclear bombs, didn't beg for sympathy or aid. It rebuilt itself with pride and an unshakeable sense of self-respect*. In the years since, it has never once stretched out a hand to America for alms.

An Indian man living in Japan for over a decade was about to leave Japan for good. He observed during his stay that no Japanese ever discussed or asked him much about India!

So, he had been a bit curious and asked his closest Japanese friend prior to departure: *What Japanese think about India & Indians in general?*

After a long pause, the friend replied, 
*"We are taught Indian history... not for inspiration, but as a warning."*

Confused, the Indian man asked, "A warning?"

"*Tell me," the Japanese friend continued, "how many British ruled India?"*
The Indian man thought, "Perhaps... around 10,000?"
The Japanese man nodded grimly. "And how many Indians lived there? Over 300 million, right?"
"Then who oppressed your people? Who carried out the orders to whip, torture, and shoot them?" he pressed. 

"*When General Dyer gave the command 'Fire!*' *at Jallianwala Bagh, who pulled the trigger?* The soldiers weren't British; they were Indian."
"Not one turned their rifle on the tyrant. Not one," he said. "*You want to talk about slavery? That was your real slavery. Not of the body, but of the soul."*

The Indian man stood frozen, silent, and ashamed.

*The Japanese friend went on, "How many Mughals came from Central Asia? A few thousand maybe?* And yet they ruled you for centuries. They built empires not with their numbers, but because *your own people bowed their heads and offered their loyalty in exchange for survival... or silver."*

"*Your own people converted. Your own brothers became instruments of their oppression. Your own men handed over your heroes*. Chandrashekhar Azad was betrayed. Bhagat Singh faced the gallows without even a whisper of help from those who called themselves patriots," he said.

"*You don't need foreign enemies. YOUR OWN PEOPLE BETRAY YOU AGAIN AND AGAIN FOR POWER, POSITION, AND PERSONAL GAIN. That is why we keep our distance.*"

"*When the British came to Hong Kong and Singapore, not one native man joined their army. But in India, you didn’t just join the enemy. You served them.* Worshipped them. Killed your own people to please them."

"*Even today, you haven’t changed*. Offer some free electricity, a bottle of liquor, a blanket—and your vote, your conscience, your voice are all sold without a second thought. *YOUR LOYALTY LIES NOT WITH YOUR NATION, BUT WITH YOUR STOMACH*," he said.

"You chant slogans. You march in protests. But when the country needs your character, where are you? YOUR FIRST LOYALTY IS STILL TO YOURSELF AND YOUR FAMILY. EVERYTHING ELSE —SOCIETY, DHARMA, THE COUNTRY —CAN BURN."

*He ended with one final statement:*
"If your nation is not strong, your home will never be safe. If your character is weak, no flag can protect you."

*This is not mockery. It is a mirror.*

Perhaps the time has come for us to stop looking away, because India doesn’t need more patriots in speeches. *IT NEEDS CITIZENS OF UNSHAKEABLE CHARACTER. NOT JUST FREEDOM FIGHTERS, BUT FREEDOM KEEPERS. NOT JUST FLAGS IN OUR HANDS, BUT LOYALTY IN OUR HEARTS*.

It is bitter. But it is true.

HOPE It Shakes our conscience and please spread the word

text:
Today in History 
October 11th
2025
Diane Keaton Dies of Bacterial Pneumonia at 79

Hollywood lost one of its most beloved and distinctive stars when Diane Keaton died on October 11, 2025, at the age of 79, in California. Her death was attributed to primary bacterial pneumonia, according to her death certificate. The news shocked fans and fellow entertainers around the world, marking the end of an extraordinary career that spanned more than five decades. Known for her unmistakable voice, infectious laughter, unconventional fashion, and unforgettable performances, Keaton leaves behind a remarkable legacy in American cinema.

Born Diane Hall on January 5, 1946, in Los Angeles, California, she was the eldest of four children. Her father, John Newton Ignatius Hall, worked in real estate and civil engineering, while her mother, Dorothy Deanne Keaton, was a homemaker and amateur photographer. Growing up in Santa Ana, California, Diane developed an early passion for performing, particularly acting and singing.

After briefly attending college, she moved to New York City to pursue her dreams. She adopted her mother’s maiden name, Keaton, because another performer was already registered under Diane Hall. She studied acting at the Neighborhood Playhouse and made her Broadway debut in the musical Hair in 1968.

Her breakthrough came when she appeared in Woody Allen’s Broadway production of Play It Again, Sam, which earned her a Tony Award nomination. Her collaboration with Allen would become one of Hollywood’s most recognizable creative partnerships.

In 1972, Keaton achieved widespread recognition portraying Kay Adams, the girlfriend and eventual wife of Michael Corleone, played by Al Pacino, in Francis Ford Coppola’s masterpiece The Godfather. She reprised the role in The Godfather Part II in 1974 and The Godfather Part III in 1990.

Her defining moment arrived in 1977 with Annie Hall, the romantic comedy directed by Woody Allen. Her portrayal of the charming, independent, and wonderfully eccentric Annie earned her the Academy Award for Best Actress. The film also transformed her into a fashion icon, popularizing oversized blazers, men’s ties, hats, and relaxed, masculine-inspired clothing.

Throughout the following decades, Keaton demonstrated remarkable versatility. She received additional Academy Award nominations for Reds (1981), Marvin’s Room (1996), and Something’s Gotta Give (2003).

Audiences also embraced her performances in Baby Boom, Father of the Bride, The First Wives Club, The Family Stone, and Book Club. Whether portraying a struggling mother, a heartbroken wife, or a woman rediscovering love later in life, Keaton brought warmth, vulnerability, intelligence, and humor to every character.

Beyond acting, Keaton was an accomplished director, producer, photographer, author, and passionate admirer of architecture and interior design. Her memoirs offered personal reflections on family, aging, relationships, and the challenges of navigating Hollywood while remaining true to herself.

Although she had high-profile relationships with Woody Allen, Warren Beatty, and Al Pacino, Keaton never married. Instead, she embraced motherhood later in life, adopting her daughter Dexter in 1996 and her son Duke in 2001. She frequently described raising her children as one of the most meaningful experiences of her life.

Her contributions to entertainment were recognized with numerous honors, including the American Film Institute’s Life Achievement Award in 2017.

Away from the spotlight, Keaton was known for her affection for animals and her support of people experiencing homelessness. Following her death, her family encouraged admirers to honor her memory through donations to animal shelters and local food banks.

I’m 29F, and last Christmas, I paid $2,400 to rent a cabin so my family could spend four days together.

Nobody offered to split it. That’s fine. I make more than most of them, and I wanted us to have a nice Christmas.

She asked if I could cover her car payment because she was short $680.

I said no.

I said no because three weeks earlier, she’d posted pictures from a weekend in Miami. New outfits, expensive dinners, the whole thing. When I asked her about it, she laughed and said, “Girl, I needed a break.”

Now she needed me to cover a bill she’d known about all month.

text:
Today in History
October 11th
1910
Theodore Roosevelt Becomes the First U.S. President to Fly in an Airplane

On October 11, 1910, former President Theodore Roosevelt made aviation history when he became the first person who had served as President of the United States to fly in a powered airplane. The historic flight took place at Kinloch Field near St. Louis, Missouri, with pioneering aviator Archibald “Arch” Hoxsey piloting a Wright Brothers-built aircraft. Although the flight lasted only about four minutes, it marked an important milestone in American aviation history.

Roosevelt, who served as the nation’s 26th president from 1901 to 1909, was renowned for his adventurous spirit, physical courage, and enthusiasm for innovation. His interests included exploration, hunting, military affairs, and scientific advancement. Although no longer president, he remained one of America’s most influential public figures.

The flight occurred during an aviation exhibition at Kinloch Field, when powered flight was still a relatively new achievement. The Wright Brothers had completed their first successful powered flight at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, less than seven years earlier, on December 17, 1903. Airplanes remained experimental, fragile, and dangerous, making public demonstrations both thrilling and unpredictable.

Arch Hoxsey, an accomplished pilot with the Wright Brothers’ exhibition team, invited Roosevelt to accompany him into the air. According to the Smithsonian Institution, Roosevelt initially declined but quickly reconsidered and enthusiastically accepted.

With Hoxsey at the controls, Roosevelt climbed aboard the open aircraft before an astonished crowd. The airplane rose approximately 150 feet above the ground and completed two circuits of the airfield during its four-minute flight.

Hoxsey performed several steep climbs and dives, giving Roosevelt an especially exciting introduction to aviation. The former president waved enthusiastically to spectators below, prompting Hoxsey to warn him to hold on securely.

After landing, Roosevelt expressed tremendous enjoyment and reportedly regretted that his schedule prevented him from staying airborne longer. His willingness to embrace the risks of early aviation reinforced his reputation for courage and adventure.

Roosevelt had been visiting Missouri to support Republican candidates and arrived at the airfield accompanied by Governor Herbert S. Hadley. Photographers documented the extraordinary occasion, capturing Roosevelt seated beside Hoxsey in the exposed aircraft. Early motion-picture footage of the flight was also recorded and is preserved by the Library of Congress.

The achievement attracted considerable public attention, helping demonstrate the growing possibilities of powered flight. At a time when many Americans still viewed airplanes as dangerous curiosities, Roosevelt’s participation offered a powerful endorsement of aviation’s potential.

Tragically, Hoxsey’s pioneering career ended less than three months later. On December 30, 1910, he established an altitude record of 11,474 feet in Los Angeles. The following day, he was killed in an airplane crash while attempting another high-altitude flight, underscoring the enormous dangers faced by early aviators.

Roosevelt’s historic journey represented more than a daring adventure. It symbolized the connection between American leadership and an emerging technology destined to transform transportation, military operations, and international relations.

Although Roosevelt was a former president when he flew, his achievement established an important presidential aviation milestone. In subsequent decades, aircraft evolved from experimental machines into essential instruments of government transportation and national defense, eventually making presidential air travel routine.

text:
💍 🔭 A smoke ring in the Swan
Slide down the Swan's neck from Deneb on an October evening, stop just southwest of the faint star 39 Cygni, and in that dense river of suns a tiny red ring floats on its own, smaller than many of the stars around it. It is what is left of a star much like our Sun, which ran out of fuel, swelled, and breathed its outer layers into space. NGC 6894, the Little Ring Nebula, shines at magnitude 12.3 and spans less than a fortieth of the full Moon.

The red glow is hydrogen and nitrogen lit by the ultraviolet of the exposed core, a white dwarf near magnitude 18 sitting in the hole of the ring, while the faint blue-green haze comes from oxygen. No black hole; the star was never heavy enough. Deep images show faint streaks to the northwest, gas stripped from its halo as the nebula drifts through the Milky Way.

📏 How big is 1.1 light-years?
An airliner at 900 km/h would need about 1.3 million years to cross it, and you would have to line up some 27 million Earth to Moon distances to span it. Its famous neighbour M57 in Lyra looks twice as wide and about 25 times brighter, so this little cousin is often passed by. 🤷‍♂️

🕙 When and how
From central Europe it climbs to about 70° in the south. In October it culminates around 20:45 and stays well placed until midnight. Visually, a 5-inch refractor, like the 🇺🇸 Televue NP127is or the 🇯🇵 Takahashi TOA-130, at 150x shows a small pale disk, and an OIII filter with steady air hints at the darker centre.

🇩🇪 A small confession. My country, Germany, once gave the world Zeiss refractors, yet today it has very little left to offer us small amateurs in this trade, so we import high-class optics from those who still build them, and a similar story plays out with our AI. Many of us make our own electricity on the rooftop (I put a telescope up there instead 😂) and some run large language models at home, a special approach. As a Greek I have the right to open my mouth; democracy wins, the first thing we learn as kids at school in Greece 😉. So, mostly imported glass for us small amateurs. Back to the point, guys.

📷 The capture
This frame came from my 🇫🇷 Vaonis Vespera II #smarttelescope, the 50 mm f/5 quadruplet screwed onto the roof tiles 20 m above ground, on a hill at 340 m, with the whole sky open all night while I sleep. At 250 mm the ring spans under twenty pixels, a field portrait rather than a close-up, yet shell and blue halo already separate.

🏺 When the light left
Around 3400 BC scribes in Uruk were pressing the first signs of writing into wet clay, mostly to count grain and sheep. Egypt was still a patchwork of rival chiefdoms. Farmers built pile dwellings on Lake Constance, and a little later Ötzi crossed the Alpine ice with a copper axe and never came back.

🌍 The Earth's clock
In geological terms 5,400 years is a heartbeat inside the Holocene, the mild stretch since the last ice age. Coastlines looked almost as they do today, the North Sea had long covered Doggerland, and the Sahara was still slowly turning from grassland with lakes, hippos and giraffes into desert as the monsoon withdrew south.

Oak, lime and hazel forests covered central Europe, home to aurochs, elk, wolves and brown bears, with beavers shaping every valley. Far north, on Wrangel Island, the last woolly mammoths were still grazing, and they would outlast the first pyramids of Egypt.

✨ Our Sun's future
I like this one for its modesty, one star's last breath almost lost among the clouds of Cygnus, and a quiet preview of where our own Sun is heading some five billion years from now.

text:
Europe’s Moment of Truth – Lessons from the Ukrainian Ex-Foreign Minister’s Wake-Up Call

Geopolitical reality leaves no room for illusions. In a candid and alarming interview, former Ukrainian Foreign Minister Dmytro Kuleba made it unequivocally clear that Europe is facing a historic existential crisis. His key points serve as an urgent appeal to the European Union to finally shed its naivety regarding security policy.

The Illusion of Security and the Kremlin’s Calculus

A central point of Kuleba’s warning is this:

“We don’t need to drag the Germans into it. Putin will drag you into a war.”

With this statement, the former top diplomat challenges the fear prevalent among parts of the European public that Western support measures might be what drags the continent into war in the first place. Instead, he makes it unmistakably clear that the Russian aggressor is pursuing long-term, destructive goals aimed at the entire European model of peace.

In doing so, Kuleba sharply criticizes a fundamental European misconception: while Western political culture is based on the principle of "win-win" outcomes and a willingness to compromise, Vladimir Putin operates according to the logic of victory and defeat. For the Kremlin, there are no diplomatic gray areas in this conflict—only the subjugation or destruction of the adversary.

The Danger of Nationalism and Isolationism (The AfD’s Fallacy)

While right-wing and populist forces—such as the AfD in Germany—try to convince citizens that retreating into the nation-state and acting alone offers protection, reality demonstrates the exact opposite.  Individual states are too weak: In a world of great powers and ruthless autocrats, isolated nation-states carry no geopolitical weight.

Europe as the only shield: The solution lies not in fragmentation, but in a united Europe capable of decisive action. Only by acting together do EU states possess the economic, political, and demographic strength to be taken seriously as global players.

What Europe needs now: Politicians with courage.

According to Kuleba’s analysis, the European Union’s main problem is not a lack of prosperity or resources, but a lack of political courage.

Europe needs leaders willing to ruffle feathers, speak unpopular truths, and make uncomfortable decisions.

The tendency to hesitate and wait until crises directly strike European democracies physically costs lives every day and weakens our own defenses.

Conclusion

We must finally draw the necessary conclusions from the warnings issued by the former Ukrainian foreign minister. Europe must not wait until the war reaches its own borders. The European Union must act as a united front, drastically boost its defense capabilities, and abandon the deluded belief that lasting peace with despots can be achieved through mere appeasement. We are Europe—but that strength is only valuable if we deploy it with determination and unity.

text:
From a commentary on Haggai by Cyril of Alexandria, bishop
My name is great among the nations

When our Savior came, he appeared as a divine temple, glorious beyond any comparison, far more splendid and excellent than the older temple. He exceeded the old as much as worship in Christ and the gospels exceeds the cult of the laws, as much as truth exceeds its shadows.

Furthermore, I might point out that originally there was just one temple at Jerusalem, in which one people, the Israelites, offered their sacrifices. Since the only-begotten Son became like us, and as Scripture says, though he was Lord and God, he has shone upon us, the rest of the world has been filled with places of worship. Now there are countless worshipers who honor the universal God with spiritual offerings and fragrant sacrifices. This, surely, is what Malachi foretold, speaking, as if in the person of God: I am a great king, says the Lord; my name is honored among the nations, and everywhere there is offered to my name the fragrance of a pure sacrifice.

With justice, therefore, do we say that the final temple, the Church, will be more glorious. To those who are so solicitous for the Church and labor for its construction, Haggai declares that a gift will be made, a gift from heaven given by the Savior. That gift is Christ himself, the peace of all men; through him we have access in the one Spirit to the Father. The prophet goes on to say: I will give peace to this place and peace of soul to save all who lay the foundation to rebuild the temple. Christ too says somewhere: My peace I give you. Paul will teach how profitable this is for those who love: The peace of Christ, he says, which surpasses all understanding will keep your minds and hearts. Isaiah, the seer, made the same prayer: O Lord our God, give us peace, for you have given us everything. Once a man has been found worthy of Christ’s peace, he can easily save his soul and guide his mind to carry out exactingly the demands of virtue.

Haggai, therefore, declares that peace will be given to all who build. One builds the Church either as a teacher of the sacred mysteries, as one set over the house of God, or as one who works for his own good by setting himself forth as a living and spiritual stone in the holy temple, God’s dwelling place in the Spirit. The results of these efforts will profit such men so that each will be able to gain his own salvation without difficulty.

text:
Ukraine is not hitting Russian refineries for fun. It is hitting them because those plants turn crude into diesel, jet fuel, and gasoline that keep Russian tanks, trucks, aircraft, and occupation logistics running.

A country that launched a full-scale war of aggression does not get a protected energy sector. Under the law of armed conflict, objects that make an effective contribution to military action and whose destruction offers a definite military advantage are military objectives. Refineries feeding the Russian war machine meet that test.

Russia has spent years striking Ukrainian power plants, substations, dams, ports, and heating systems in winter. Moscow does not get to demand immunity for its own fuel system while it tries to freeze and black out Ukrainian cities.

Diesel prices are a real political problem. They are not a legal veto. If higher pump prices were enough to outlaw strikes on an aggressor’s war fuel, every defender would have to fight with one hand tied so distant markets stayed comfortable.

Trump can ask Kyiv to spare refineries. That is a policy preference about inflation and talks. It is not a finding that the targets are illegitimate.

To the people of Ukraine, striking the oil refineries fueling the war against their country is a matter of national survival. For Washington, the political concern is whether those strikes will drive up diesel prices in the United States ahead of the midterms. Those priorities are not morally equivalent.

Zelensky’s job is to degrade Russia’s ability to keep killing Ukrainians, not to manage global product balances for Washington.

If the United States wants those strikes to stop, the serious path is a real energy-for-energy halt: Russia stops hitting Ukrainian infrastructure, Ukraine pauses refinery strikes, with verification. Begging only Ukraine to stand down while Russia keeps firing is not neutrality. It is asking the victim to subsidize the invader’s fuel supply.

Ukraine has the right to hit the refineries that power the army occupying its land. That right does not disappear because diesel is expensive.

text:
I usually write about artificial intelligence here. But today I want to tell you who I am and why I chose this path.

I was born in Ukraine. I was 21 when Russia launched its full-scale invasion.

I volunteered to defend my home.

We fought without official registration or salaries. We had Chinese-made tourniquets that sometimes snapped right before our eyes. We used pieces of cloth to stop the bleeding because sometimes that was all we had.

I won’t pretend I went to war without hatred. I hated the Russian invaders who came to destroy our homes.

I lost my friends, my parents, and my sisters. I was left alone.

I was severely wounded myself. For a long time, I didn’t know whether I would survive or ever walk again.

But I’m still here.

I believe the universe gave me a second life. I’ve accepted that I cannot bring back the people I lost, and I’m trying to live this new life to the fullest.

Yesterday, October 10, Trump said Ukraine needs a new president.

I agree that my country needs political change. But my reasons come from what I’ve experienced, not from Washington.

There are things I witnessed that I haven’t spoken about publicly. I’m afraid that telling the whole story could have serious consequences for me.

My parents taught me to be honest with myself and others, to do good, and to treat people with love.

I haven’t forgotten those lessons.

Russia has enormous resources and military power. But I’ve seen what Ukrainians are capable of when they’re defending their own homes. I believe we can win.

What hurts is seeing corruption and impunity destroy the motivation of people who have already sacrificed so much.

American journalists have asked to interview me. People have offered help. I’ve refused. I’ve never wanted my suffering to become a way of asking for money or attention.

Those who know me understand what I’ve survived and why I have so much to say.

I know my views can make me inconvenient for people in power.

And perhaps now you’ll understand why I chose artificial intelligence.

I’m interested in AI safety because I know what happens when power is used without responsibility.

I could devote my abilities to building weapons. But I don’t want to create more suffering.

I want to build something useful. Something that helps protect people.

I have already seen enough death.

I want this war to end. I want those responsible for crimes to face justice. And I want ordinary people to have the chance to live peacefully.

I was given a second life.

I don’t want to waste it on hatred.

text:
When the war began, they offered him a way out of Kyiv. He stayed. For more than four years, he has led a country living under the sound of sirens. 

Ukraine ultimately discovered a weapon that significantly impacted Russia: drone attacks on its oil refineries. These strikes were so effective that Russia had to halt diesel exports. The repercussions, however, were felt elsewhere: diesel prices in the U.S. surged above six dollars per gallon shortly before the midterm elections, with Washington attributing the increase to Ukraine. 

Trump urged Zelensky six times to cease the strikes. Each time, Zelensky prioritized the war over American fuel concerns. Consequently, Trump shifted his approach, reaching an agreement on diesel supplies with Putin, the Kremlin leader bombing Ukraine, and declared that Ukraine requires new leadership. 

Currently, Zelensky faces a dilemma. If he halts the strikes, Russia will have a peaceful winter to target Ukraine’s power grid, leaving people without electricity. If he continues, he risks losing the crucial Western support and weaponry that sustain Ukraine. Holding an election presents another challenge: it would take place amid ongoing war, with soldiers voting from trenches and many families still abroad. He rose to fame portraying an ordinary man who becomes president. Now, he's an ordinary man watching others determine his fate.

text:
Of course, what is truly sickening, is that Boris Johnson who is largely personally responsible for the ongoing war in Ukraine, has the audacity to continue commenting on the war. 

Had it not been for the intervention of Boris Johnson and influential figures in Washington, including Victoria Nuland, Ukraine might have had a genuine opportunity to end this catastrophic war in the spring of 2022, before the destruction and loss of life reached their present proportions.

The possibility of a negotiated settlement was not imaginary. Ukrainian and Russian negotiators had made substantial progress in Istanbul. Ukraine had indicated its willingness to accept permanent neutrality in exchange for binding international security guarantees. Questions concerning Crimea and Donbas could potentially have been addressed through separate negotiations.

Yet rather than energetically pursuing this diplomatic opening, Western governments increasingly embraced the prospect of confronting and weakening Russia through continued Ukrainian resistance. Johnson’s intervention in Kyiv in April 2022 reflected that approach, encouraging Zelensky to resist Putin rather than pursue an accommodation.

Nor was Istanbul the first missed opportunity. In December 2021, Russia had demanded negotiations over NATO enlargement and European security arrangements. Washington rejected Moscow’s demand for a veto over Ukrainian NATO membership, although it offered discussions on other security issues. Whether a more imaginative diplomatic response could have averted the invasion remains an important and insufficiently examined question.

None of this absolves Putin of responsibility for invading Ukraine. But acknowledging Russia’s responsibility does not absolve Western governments of responsibility for their own decisions, particularly when those decisions may have narrowed opportunities for peace.

The tragedy is that diplomacy was treated increasingly as an obstacle to military objectives rather than as the indispensable means of ending the slaughter.

We cannot know whether the Istanbul negotiations would ultimately have succeeded. But the possibility that a negotiated settlement might have spared Ukraine years of devastation deserves serious scrutiny, not dismissal

text:
Ensi Silaqi — The Jade Blade of Labelas

Born among the forgotten jungles of the Feathered Vale, Ensi Silaqi inherited an ancient tradition practiced by few: the Sublime Way, where martial discipline could elevate swordsmanship into something approaching the supernatural.

But Ensi sought to go further.

Her journey led her across impossible cliffs to a sealed temple guarded by Itzama, the Feathered Protector. There, under the serpent’s watchful gaze and the mysterious Old Man’s guidance, Ensi learned to weave the Sublime Way with the hidden mysteries of the Wu Jen, becoming a warrior who could blend steel and spell with devastating precision.

That training would make her an invaluable member of the Heroes of Hommlet.

Against the undead hordes of Nulb, her katana flashed once—and an entire horde fell in two, consumed by fire before her companions could even draw their weapons.

Yet Ensi’s greatest trial was not a battlefield.

Separated from her friends, she glimpsed a terrible secret: a colossal cage bound in chains, watched by a Solar whose whispered warning changed everything.

“We need to kill The First.”

The Heroes fought, suffered, and ultimately saved the world—but The First escaped. Ensi never forgot what she had seen.

In her final years, she returned to Itzama’s temple. Offered eternal rest among the Seldarine, she chose instead to remain beside the sealed sanctuary, guarding secrets she could only pray would never be unleashed.

When her mortal flame finally faded, the heavens answered. Ensi rose again as a Sacred Watcher, forever standing guard beside Itzama.

Some warriors are remembered for the enemies they defeat. Ensi Silaqi is remembered for the secret she chose to protect.

🗡️ The blade may rest. The watch never ends.

text:
A tribe suing over an exclusive license is the story that matters here, because it shows how much of this business sits in paperwork rather than the odds board. I read the paperwork first, and the other stories here only back that up.

1 - The Seminole Tribe of Florida filed a 72-page complaint in Broward County alleging @DraftKings is running an illegal gambling operation that violates @HardRockBet's exclusive license, with CEO Jason Robins also sued personally. Exclusivity is clearly worth a lot of paper.

2 - @Polymarket is taking the Dutch gambling regulator to court over its ban, arguing it sells derivatives and shouldn't be treated as a betting site, according to Cointelegraph. I know a bet when I see one.

3 - Kick_Champ claims Twitch streamer @MitchJonez leaked his Rainbet casino deal, which it says is worth $150 million a year. Worth remembering the next time a streamer sounds thrilled about a casino.

4 - Democratic nominee @KeishaBottoms supports a statewide vote on casino gambling and goes further, casting legalization as an economic development tool for struggling communities, per @ajc. I've heard that pitch before.

5 - THE $136,717 WITHDRAWAL BLOCK

@0xJinxer claims @Stake blocked his $136,717 withdrawal over a wagering requirement he says he had already completed. He alleges the block was caused by a bug Stake knew about a month earlier. Everything turns on that wagering requirement and whether the operator's own system counted it correctly. A bug known for a month, followed by a player's money held behind it, is indefensible, and I'd put that on the operator, not the player. Screenshot your wagering progress before you request any large withdrawal. We've all learned that one the hard way.

6 - NO-WAGERING RAKEBACK WINDOW

@PlayOnMint ran 25% rakeback for 5 days from Oct 5, paid instantly in the currency played. The line that decides it is that the rakeback carries no wagering requirement, which is the first thing I look for in any rakeback. Play in the window also still counts toward the $MNTD airdrop allocation, the daily drip claim and the NFT WL. Instant payout with no strings is the standard every rakeback offer should be held to, and this one meets it. If an operator won't offer that, I read the rakeback as a bonus in disguise.
